subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LEGALIZE INCREASE IN POSTAL RATES- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of great urgency and pressing necessity. Yesterday the House of Commons unanimously concurred in the fourth report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, declaring that the raising of postal rates other than by amendments to the Post Office Act is invalid. Inasmuch as the joint committee is the watchdog of the rights of parliament, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale):
That the House direct the Postmaster General to obey the will of parliament by introducing amendments to the Post Office Act to legalize the arbitrary action taken in raising postal rates on April 1, and table the judicial decision on which he says his decision is based.

The empirical evidence demonstrates that the federal government has not improved the economic position of the poor relative to the highest income families.

subtopic: ALLEGATION INCREASE IN POSTAL RATES ILLEGAL
speechtext: Everything which has been done by the Postmaster General has been done on the assumption that it was legal, on legal advice. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice: it concerns the evidence given over the last two days by assistant commissioner Thomas Venner, head of the criminal investigation department of the RCMP. If a policeman did not have enough evidence to obtain a search warrant from a judge, a warrantless search could be in the public interest because it could help detect crime.
That was the evidence given before the McDonald inquiry. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ILLEGAL ACTIVITIES OF RCMP-APPLICATION OF RULE OF LAW
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have been saying for many years, certainly since the conduct of the RCMP was brought into question or the conduct of some members of the RCMP was questioned, that the mandate of the RCMP, its members and officers, was clearly to live within the law and under the rule of law. The McDonald commission is inquiring into incidents where the law might not have been followed; that is the purpose of the inquiry. I do not think that as a result of each day's revelations it would be useful for me or the Solicitor General to send them a new directive to live within the law: it has been made very clear that that is the government's instruction to members of the force.

speechtext:
I take it from the answer that there has been no specific direction by either the minister or his counterpart. My question is this: In view of the fact that there has now been sufficient admission, not merely in the Venner evidence but in the evidence of many other senior officers in the RCMP, that a prima facie criminal act has taken place, and in view of the minister's responsibility as the chief law enforcement officer of Canada, why has he not moved to lay charges against those persons who have admittedly broken the criminal law, since
[Mr. Basford.1

evidence is available to him? Is this not a breach of the minister's duty to the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ILLEGAL ACTIVITIES OF RCMP-APPLICATION OF RULE OF LAW
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are following the practice which has been followed in inquiries of a similar nature in the past, such as the Norris royal commission and others. That is the practice we are following in this inquiry. In the case of the Norris inquiry, for example, there were allegations each day of criminality or alleged criminality. At the conclusion of the Norris inquiry, that evidence was referred by the law officers of the Crown to the appropriate provincial attorneys general for action.

speechtext: Order, please. The matter was raised just recently in an opposite context, but it had to do with fund raising and the use of the frank. The House is aware that the frank replaces the postage stamp for members of the House of Commons, and the same privilege extends to the public in communicating with their elected members. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening I referred to a document put out by Peter Henry

Jerch and Associates of Winnipeg, a financial consulting firm, which assists Canadian businesses to move out of Canada. At the present time they are acting on behalf of 64 businesses that are planning to move due to the political climate created by the Liberal government over the last ten years. In a document he sent to me, Mr. Jerch writes as follows:
Countries or for that matter provinces which have nationalistic, leftist or extremely strong bureaucratic tendencies make striving and successful entrepreneurs feel uncomfortable.
They do not feel comfortable in Canada. That is why Canada is the greatest boost to the United States economy today. States are fighting among themselves as to which one will be called the eleventh province. Kentucky was first to ask that they become the eleventh province. In today's paper the State of Florida says that they are the eleventh province. These states will have to get in line, Mr. Speaker. Kentucky claimed first that they were the eleventh province, and Florida will have to become the twelfth province.
Mr. Jerch points out that, through the loss of investment, jobs are lost. He gives incidents here of the number of firms which moved out of Manitoba and states that this cost 4,000 jobs in that province. In a second document supplied to me by Mr. Jerch he points out that, of the 42 firms he is dealing with, the amount of investment which is moving out of the country will cost Canada up to 13,000 jobs. These are small and medium-size businesses. Mr. Jerch is just one investment counsellor. It would be interesting to get statistics from all investment counsellors and lawyers across Canada in regard to the exact amount of money leaving Canada, together with the number of businesses which are leaving also.
Since I spoke yesterday there are more articles in today's newspapers regarding this mass exodus of capital and business leaving Canada. As I pointed out yesterday, this budget is doing nothing to keep anybody here. It is a useless document. This particular article I am looking at is headed "Florida's Sunshine Is Canada's Rain In Construction Industry". The article states:
Several Ottawa firms are among a growing number of Canadian developers providing employment for Florida construction workers.
This is occurring at a time when 166,000 Canadian construction workers, about 23 per cent of building trades work force, collect unemployment insurance.
But it's unlikely the Canadian worker would be any better off if those firms stopped their foreign projects.
"If a company deals from the heart and ends up bankrupt in five years, staying home is a worse decision" than moving to Florida, William Nevins, chief economist for the Canadian Construction Assoc., said Wednesday.
Construction companies heading south, he said, reflects a weakness in the Canadian economy. In the corporate supermarket, there are 10 times as many items in the U.S. as there are in Canada and profits are better.
This article appeared in the Ottawa Citizen, today.
As I pointed out yesterday, the Liberal members who have spoken on this budget so far have made absolutely no mention of the mass exodus of capital and business.
There is nothing in the budget. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) contributed absolutely
April 20, 1978

nothing when he spoke yesterday in this regard. He told us investment is on the increase in Canada. It is the exact opposite. Canada is no longer an attractive country in which to invest. We cannot even hold businesses or money here, never mind trying to attract additional investment funds.
When the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) spoke on this subject, all we got was a lot of smart alec cracks in his speech. He made no contribution at all on what the government will do regarding this serious problem. I have compiled considerable statistics concerning this matter over the past year.
There is another article which appeared in today's Globe and Mail. It is a report from Washington. We get more statistics on the outflow of investment from the United States than we do from Canada. The article is headed "Canadian Investments In U.S. Show A Dramatic Move Upward". The article says:
A dramatic rise in Canadian investment in the United States is indicated by figures just published by the U.S. Commerce Department.
Maybe a lot of Canadians do not understand how this affects them. It is also one of the reasons we have such record high unemployment and why unemployment is costing Canadians $8 billion a year. This amount will increase yearly, and it is because of the policies of this government and the political climate which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cohorts have created in this country over the last ten years. Many people, when they see the opinion polls and they see there is a chance that this government will be returned, will accelerate this movement of business and capital out of Canada. This is evidenced by the articles appearing daily in newspapers.
As well, the CTV television network sent a film crew to the southern United States recently, and interviewed Canadians who are moving there with their businesses and money. These people were asked why they left Canada. They answered that they left Canada because of the political uncertainty here. They put the blame on the Prime Minister. If he is returned to office in the next election, this trend will continue.
I guarantee that if this government is returned to office, Mr. Speaker, it will bring in exchange controls. Heaven help us if this government is returned to office. Canada is a country with the greatest potential in the world, and it is being destroyed by this socialistic government and its bureaucratic tendencies. This was pointed out by the investment counsellors who are assisting businesses to move out of the country. I see the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Lefebvre) is getting a chuckle out of that.
The United States commerce department statistics show Canadian direct investment in United States companies jumped by more than S500 million in 1976 to $5.9 billion. This accounts for about 10 per cent of all foreign direct investment in the United States. Only the Netherlands has a larger stake in American industry. Canadian companies and individuals had $10.67 billion invested abroad at the end of 1975. In addition to the United States, other big recipients are Brazil and Australia.
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
In Florida alone, Canadian property ownership is in excess of $450 million state wide, and Canadian development consortiums plan to spend in excess of $1.3 billion more in the next 15 years.
Here is an article from the Miami Herald. It states:
"The Canadian dollar is buying up Florida in an escalating and often frenzied scramble to find a haven from political and economical uncertainty at home ...
If we have this political uncertainty now, we will certainly have it if this government is returned again after the next election. The article goes on to say:
... Canada's largest financial and development corps alike are exporting their savings and surplus capital in a classic flight to find sanctuary.''

from this government.
In 1977 B.C. Forest Products Ltd. spent $70 million to take over a Minnesota paper company plant. Alcan Aluminum spent $140 million to take over Revere Copper and Brass in Alabama. It is too bad we could not get them to expand here and take something over in Canada.
Although statistics are hard to come by, California financial experts agree Canadian capital is flowing south in unusual volume, continuing a two-year trend that shows no sign of slackening.
The chief economist of the Royal Bank of Canada, Mr. Ralph Sultan, stated:
We have to get our house in order and make it more attractive for private capital, or else Canada will become a sleeping backwater. Capital lacks loyalty and there's not much government can do.
There is lots that the government can do. Mr. Sultan goes on to say:
Capital goes where returns are most attractive.
They are most attractive in the United States at the present time. Mr. Frank Augsbury of the St. Lawrence County Economic Council (New York), who is in Canada assisting Canadian business moving south of the border, stated:
We aren't trying to raid Canada, but if they're moving out we'll welcome them with open arms . . .
When Olympia and York Developments Ltd. of Toronto laid out $350 million in April, 1977, to buy nine skyscrapers in New York city, it became overnight the largest Canadian investor in American real estate. In addition, 26 per cent of the assets of the Trizec Corporation of Montreal ($192 million) are invested in U.S. real estate. Cadillac Fairview has invested approximately $100 million in U.S. real estate.
In Texas, and maybe that state will be the thirteenth province, a Dallas broker estimates that a quarter of a billion Canadian dollars are invested in Texas alone. In 1976, for example, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce paid $25 million for an apartment complex in Houston. Moreover, Canadian life insurance companies have acquired a half billion dollars worth of U.S. property in the last five years in Atlanta, Chicago, Denver, Los Angeles, and Philadelphia.

April 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
The governor of Louisiana was in Toronto yesterday speaking to Canadian businessmen, encouraging them to move to Louisiana. He pointed out that about $7 million or $8 million of a $2.3 billion investment in Louisiana recently came from Canada directly, and maybe $100 million indirectly. The greatest portion by far went into oil and gas ventures, he said, and most of the rest into chemical plant developments.
Next week representatives from Tennessee will be in Toronto, speaking to Canadian businessmen, assisting and encouraging them to go to the United States. The Memphis area chamber of commerce will be in Toronto next week to speak to businessmen to encourage them to move out of Canada.
I have another recent article entitled "Western Canadians Buying Into Texas, Colorado". It can easily be seen how widespread this is. We are on a disaster course in this country, but all we get is this ridiculous budget. There is absolutely nothing in it about how they are going to tackle this very serious problem and trend. Where will it end? The way we are going, all that will be left here will be the working people, the peasants and the Liberal government. The article states that they are going to Texas and Colorado as a result of political uncertainties. That is the reason behind the money exodus. All we have had in the last ten years is a lot of uncertainty in this country through the total and complete mismanagement of the nation's business by this government.
Here is another reason why many of the businesses are leaving this country:
Related to the preceding point is the problem of too much government. The ever-increasing size of the federal public service and the problems created by such expansion are factors which hinder business activity. Businessmen are forever hassled by federal regulatory agencies, boards, departments, bureaus, offices and councils with their myriad of rules, regulations, laws, edicts, orders, decrees and statements. In short, they are inundated with paper work. Moreover, should a businessman disagree with a ruling, it is extremely difficult to appeal to these bodies and the time and effort involved usually preclude an appeal anyway.
That is not the way they operate in the United States. That is why they are clearing out of Canada. In the February 28 edition of the Ottawa Citizen, Neil Wood, president of Cadillac Fairview Ltd., is quoted as saying:
We're not selling out Canadian assets, nor turning our back on good Canadian opportunties, but they are few and far between. Government delays in getting approvals continue to frustrate us in Canada compared with U.S. where development is welcome.
This matter has been raised a number of times. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and the Minister of Finance were questioned about what action they were going to take to encourage business and investment to stay in Canada. We did not get cut answers. They will not even sit down and talk to these people to encourage them to stay here. They bring in a meaningless budget, thinking that will be the answer.
Government involvement in the economy has increased to the point where 42 per cent of our gross national product, the sum of all goods and services produced in Canada, is produced by the government. If present trends by provincial and federal

governments continue, 88 per cent of all goods and services produced in Canada by 1990 will be under the state, and only 12 per cent will be left for private enterprise. In policy making, the only thing the Trudeau government can think of is socialism. For example, if oil prices rise, they set up a national petroleum corporation. The solution to the problem is to reduce the size of government slowly, not through mass layoffs of dedicated civil servants, but by attrition. In addition, wasteful make-work projets could be eliminated. If governments want to make work, the best way to do it is through proper incentives to private industry. That is something this government does not want to do.
It is very strange when we question the Prime Minister and others on this. What are their motives that they do not want to deal with this problem or talk about it? When they bring in a budget, there is nothing in it to indicate how they intend to deal with this very serious trend.
With regard to our very serious inflation which has been caused by this government, Milton Friedman, Nobel Prize Laureate in Economics, stated:
There is only one place where inflation is made in Canada and that is Ottawa. The unions don't make inflation for a very simple reason; the unions do not own a printing press on which they can turn out those multi-coloured pieces of paper called money. The reason you have inflation is because the government has been printing too much and spending too much.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Lessard (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At this early stage of my intervention, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal briefly with some of the remarks which the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) has just made, for he is well known in the House for his severe criticisms of the government generally, but more specifically of the right hon. Prime Minister. I suggest that his repeated attacks against our Prime Minister form a personal vendetta against him; for this reason, I do not think he will gain much support from the Canadian public because politicians seeking revenge are not likely to convince a great many people.
If I have a piece of advice for the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, it is to limit his criticisms to the course of action people take and not to the people themselves, because behaving the way he does now will not improve his position.
Mr. Speaker, we are going into the last day of the debate on the budget brought down on April 10 last by the Hon. Jean Chretien, an occasion on which I should like to congratulate our colleague for his first budget, which we all recognize as having been difficult to prepare. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, few Canadians expected to receive great gifts; aware as they are of the economic situation of their country, Canadians expected the Minister of Finance to be responsible and present them with adjustments to the fiscal situation as it stands; they did not expect him to make any great concessions, neither in the field of taxes nor in that of new programs requiring additional
April 20, 1978

government expenditures. That, Mr. Speaker, because Canadians realize that in years past the Canadian government made considerable effort to increase expenditures to give new impetus to our economy, and those substantial expenditures, added to tax cuts, personal and corporate, resulted in the growth of our national debt.
For the year just ended we have incurred a deficit of more than $8 billion. For the year which begins, with the new budget brought forward and the few concessions made, the deficit of Canada will probably exceed the $11.5 billion mark. It is obvious that with so little elbow room the Minister of Finance could not, and the Canadian people recognized this, give substantial income tax cuts to Canadian consumers in particular nor could he increase substantially the expenditures in the areas which could have contributed to reduce unemployment. He did so, however, by rearranging some existing measures in order to increase their impact on the development of our economy.
This budget, Mr. Speaker, was well received and perceived by responsible people both in the press and in industry as a whole. It was well perceived because it has been seen as the result of both an in-depth study by officials from the Department of Finance and of an objective decision from the minister and the government in the face of our responsibilities. Even though an election will probably be called soon, we did not want either to take measures which could have been interpreted as a step aimed at gaining the electorate's favour, because it would have increased our deficit. We are aware that Canadian voters recognize the work that has been done by this government and we are sure that they will make the right judgement when the election is called. I am personally aware of it and so are my colleagues. And as even the previous speaker said, the polls that have been taken indicate beyond any doubt that the Liberal party and Pierre Elliott Trudeau's government will be returned to office.
Mr. Speaker, we can say about this budget that, in spite of the financial limits the minister was facing, he succeeded in proposing measures likely to increase the general demand of our economy. On one hand, federal participation in the sales tax cut would increase consumption and benefit all Canadian consumers. On the other hand, other measures such as those related to research and development, to energy development activities, to investments in the railway system would represent incentives to the general industrial growth of Canada. Finally, maintaining for another year the tariff reductions established in 1973 on a wide range of consumer goods would avoid the higher retail prices those goods would otherwise have shown, and therefore would benefit all Canadian consumers.
Following the discussions held during the recent meetings between federal and provincial governments, meetings which, as you are aware, were held in December and January and
The Budget-Mr. Lessard
have culminated in a federal-provincial conference of first ministers in February, it became apparent that the involvement and co-operation of all sectors were a necessity in a number of areas.
The budget introduced on April 10 represents an important step toward sharing responsibilities between the two levels of government in so far as the stabilization policy and, more particularly at this time, the stimulation of the economy are concerned. Of course, measures like those related to research and development activities as well as the development of energy can potentially benefit all parts of Canada and might possibly benefit some provinces more than others. However, it is through more specific action, and I am thinking here of the grants for the retail sales tax cut, that the federal government, despite financial constraints and the need to boost the economy in general, has shown its concern with the importance of regional problems. On the one hand, this action is indeed very favourable to the Atlantic provinces, which will have nothing to pay for the sales tax cut and will therefore not bear any additional tax burden. On the other hand, this action will also be greatly beneficial not only to Quebec consumers but also to the producers of that province where a high percentage of Canadian manufactured goods are produced.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that during the current negotiations, the Quebec government will recognize the usefulness of the proposal put forth by the federal government and the Minister of Finance, and that it will agree to take part, with the other Canadian provinces, in the effort to reduce the impact on consumers of the provincial retail sales tax. And I do think that the fact that this proposal was accepted, and the Quebec decision to cut even more the sales tax on certain products, is a direct recognition of the negative impact the rentail sales tax has on the general economy. When one considers that first analyses on the potential impact of that tax cut, and indications are that in Quebec more than 10,000 jobs would be created rapidly following those sales tax reductions, one realizes, Mr. Speaker, the impact the role of the provinces has on the development of the federal and provincial economies, the responsibility as a result of the tax tool they have to influence the creation of jobs in Canada and on their territories. They have proven, Mr. Speaker, that they have a role to play in fighting unemployment and that it is not only the responsibility of the federal government to come up with measures to create jobs and get the economy going again.
I think it is obvious that provincial governments through their budgets, their tax measures, their expenditures and their actions, also have a role to play and a very important responsibility in the performance of our economy and the rate of unemployment which is now afflicting Canada and which we here in Ottawa denounce. But the means of intervention at the federal level also have their limitations, and we want to indicate to Canadians that we are prepared to recognized and take our responsibilities and to take the necessary means to
4700

April 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Lessord
counter unemployment; but that responsibility is not incumbent only upon the federal government and must be recognized and shared by the provinces which are ever more anxious to see the federal government decentralize and give the provinces greater powers and greater revenues.
It is quite obvious that if the provinces are given greater powers and greater revenues, they will have to recognize more fully the responsibilities they have with respect to the conduct of the economy and the creation of jobs to fight unemployment. They will not be able to get more powers and then continue to believe that only the Government of Canada will be responsible for the problems and they will get the credit for the accomplishments.
The minister of finance of Quebec has just tabled his budget, and as was noticed, he anticipates in the budget that the federal government's contribution through tax transfers from the federal treasury to Quebec will exceed $3.3 billion. That is a contribution of over 25 per cent to the provincial budget, Mr. Speaker, not to mention other transfer payments from the federal government to the province of Quebec and its residents. We can be sure, Mr. Speaker, that, as some hon. members, some colleagues in the House have said before, if we compare Quebec's contribution to the Canadian economy and to the federal budget with the federal government contribution to the Quebec economy and Quebecers, I feel that, generally speaking, they are the winners. As recently as last night, when speaking to a group of citizens of Quebec, I said that when an agreement is concluded-and recently I have signed auxiliary and joint agreements with the government of Quebec-our provincial colleagues from Quebec remind us that it it a fair return of all taxes paid by Quebecers to the federal government.
I would like to take this opportunity to recall that we are at the end of April and that, as Canadian citizens, we must fill our income tax returns. As I have noted myself once again a few days ago, we all know that we pay more income tax to the Quebec government than to the federal government. And I do not know of any contribution by Quebec to federal government expenditures. Quite the opposite. Rather I note very large contributions from the federal government to the expenses of the province of Quebec and transfer payments to Quebec residents, and I pay more income tax to Quebec than I do to the federal government. And when I sign an agreement with Quebec, under all DREE programs, the minimum federal contribution is always at least 60 per cent, Mr. Speaker.
Contributions from the federal government amount to 60 per cent while those of the province are only 40 per cent. This is proof that we are pouring back more money into Quebec under our tax programs and shared cost programs than we are collecting from it. Mr. Speaker, in the October 1977 budget the finance minister also included an investment tax credit aimed at increasing the stimulating effect in DREE designated areas. The 5 per cent credit which was already in force then
[Mr. Lessard.l
and which was to expire on June 30 has been extended for three years. That credit has been raised to 7.5 per cent in certain provinces, such as Saskatchewan, Manitoba, northern Ontario and the designated areas of Quebec. In the Gaspe peninsula and the Maritime provinces their credit has been brought up to 10 per cent. Furthermore, the finance minister once again has listened to certain recommendations which we from DREE make regarding the regions. Last January he announced an employment tax credit program which is higher in DREE designated areas. In his budget, when he says that the Atlantic provinces will not have to pay back that temporary cutback of the retail sales tax, he recognizes once again the contribution of DREE toward designated areas and I think that in the name of these areas, I must thank the minister for having paid attention to the recommendations which we made to him in favour of designated areas, the areas in need of help.
Despite the financial constraints which face the government, my department has continued to undertake significant regional development initiatives. In the last fiscal year, for example, 13 new subagreements were signed, representing federal commitments of more than $377 million, and a number of amendments were made to existing subagreements. Fourteen of them increased the funding under those agreements. These amendments represent additional federal commitments of $362 million. If you add both amounts you will find that in 1977-78, under the general development agreements signed with the ten provinces, more than $739 million was committed in federal funds.
Included in the above agreements are: a new subagreement on tourism in Newfoundland; on forestry, and tourism with Sysco in Nova Scotia; an agreement to provide for further development in northeastern New Brunswick, and a second agreement on the development of agriculture in that province; major amendments to existing agreements with Quebec on agriculture, key highway networks, forest development, industrial infrastructure, and a substantial new agreement for sewage treatment facilities in Montreal; a new agreement with Alberta respecting the development of the northlands in that province; and important new agreements on industrial development, agriculture, and rural development with British Columbia.
Recently, in the current fiscal year, I signed a significant new agreement on tourism with Quebec, and other new initiatives are under discussion with various provinces at present. In fact we signed agreements with practically all the provinces. Tomorrow we will be signing an agreement with the province of Manitoba. This is the kind of collaboration and support DREE is prepared to give to provincial governments to help develop their economies.

Mr. Speaker, the department is committed in each one of the areas. Our department allocates its budgets depending on
April 20, 1978

the needs of the region. It cannot of course cover everything, but in addition to giving more to the provinces which need more, one must also consider the fact that within the framework of these agreements, we are also contributing to an extent which varies, for instance, when we commit $50 million in a province and that this amount represents 90 per cent of the expenditures, the federal effort in this province is clearly superior to what it does in another province where it also spends $50 million, but where this sum represents only 60 per cent of the expenditures, as is the case for Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I am saying this because we sometimes hear criticism from the opposition and outside the House to the effect that the departments do not allocate funds objectively in accordance with the needs of the various regions. They are forgetting that two factors are involved: the total amount allocated and also the proportion that this represents of the total expenditures of both governments under these agreements. I believe that when we consider this factor, we can better appreciate the substantial effort made in the areas which have greater disparities than others.
Since the time at our disposal is limited, I shall unfortunately have to limit my comments because I would have liked to talk about many other factors. We spent a substantial part of our budget in the Atlantic provinces, but this is because this area has much more obvious needs than other areas of Canada. I recognize that other parts of Canada also have needs, but in co-operation with the provinces, we are at least able to take care of the major priorities.
I would like to come back to Quebec in particular, Mr. Speaker, because two attitudes prevail from time to time in the House and elsewhere. Some say that the federal government is doing nothing to help Quebec fight against unemployment, to develop its economy, that we are content to observe Quebec fighting against its difficulties and that we are even pleased when we see a government like that of the Parti Quebecois have problems and that we are not in the least sympathetic to the problems and the proposals that are made.
On the other hand, when we help certain regions-and I shall prove that we do help them-others blame us and say that all federal government funds go to the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, those two positions are wrong. They are wrong because on the one hand we help the province of Quebec, this is true, but on the other hand we do everything in our power with the money at our disposal to help the government of Quebec and Quebecers particularly to get out of their present difficulties, especially as concerns unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, since I have been responsible for DREE, I have looked at what we have done in the province of Quebec. If we consider the agreements with the province of Quebec alone, on March 29, 1976 I signed four agreements with Quebec; if you sum up the share of each government they amount to a total of $162,700,000. The share of DREE or of the federal government, was $97,428,000. Those are long-term
The Budget-Mr. Lessord
commitments. On April 21, 1976 we signed another agreement in Quebec for the development of a pulp and paper mill and the federal government has committed $30 million for that project, an investment amounting to about $300 million. On June 16 another agreement was signed, this time in Mirabel for the development of the industrial park called Spicam, another $13 million commitment from the two government levels, including $8 million from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. On June 27, 1977, under the PQ government, both government levels earmarked $440 million for three agreements concerning highways, agriculture and forestry. The DREE contribution was $200,880,000.
On January 24, 1978, $77,600,000 for the industrial infrastructure, including $46 million from DREE. Recently Montreal has received $150 million for three projects. On April 6 we signed an agreement on tourism development at a cost of $76 million, including $46 million from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. So when I hear remarks to the effect that we do nothing for the province of Quebec or that we give everything to the province of Quebec, believe me, Mr. Speaker, that lack of understanding on both sides puzzles me-

speechtext:
All those amounts were committed during the fiscal year, but the spending of the cash flow is being spread, depending on the agreement signed, over a period of one to five years.

In addition to those agreements, Mr. Speaker, everyone knows there is the special area of Montreal where it has been acknowledged that there was a specific situation in the sense that over half of the Quebec unemployed are concentrated there. The cabinet has recognized that under the circumstances, in addition to the activities of other departments, my department could intervene. We have done so and to this day we have assisted more than 80 companies, new ones or older ones seeking help to expand or modernize. We are not ashamed of it, first because we are contributing to economic development and second because we are fighting against unemployment. It is part of our responsibility, but we are not the only ones involved. There is a provincial government which should play its part. Right now, I really wonder if they do so.

April 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Lessard
I see, Mr. Speaker, that the time allotted to me is slipping by and I would like to deal with other areas and not only with Quebec. In western Canada, we have signed agreements with each province. In the three prairie provinces, we have programs regularly in place to develop local infrastructures, for example in some forty communities through the prairie provinces, because we want to strengthen the structure of those communities to become growth centres through the prairies in order to hold back the population and provide services to them for the benefit of the farm industry first of all, which is very important, because when a farmer must drive 50, 60 or 100 miles to get a little service he gets discouraged and we often have seen farms deserted because of that situation. That is why the agreement on the development of local infrastructure in the prairies is a very valuable one which was signed in 1972, amended in 1975 and is presently going on. As I said, we have concluded five agreements in British Columbia during the last fiscal year and negotiations are still going on with that government. We have also concluded some agreements in Ontario as we also did in the maritimes. Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about a corporation which is under my responsibility as a minister, the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
I would be remiss if I did not mention the valuable contribution to regional development made by the Cape Breton Development Corporation. Devco took over mines which were in terrible condition in 1968. It was felt then that the only future was humane phasing out of coal mining in Cape Breton. We in the government are proud of the creative and flexible mechanism which we created. I think it is fair to say that we all owe a debt of gratitude to the present Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) who ensured that Devco would be a flexible tool. How flexible has Devco been?
Devco was able to react very quickly to changes in the world energy market, able to change policy from a phase-out of worn mines to stabilizing coal production, able to seize an opportunity to sell metallurgical coal, and able to move toward coal industry expansion to meet strong future thermal and metallurgical coal markets.
Instead of closing mines, Devco will further rehabilitate No. 26 mine and develop a major new mine over the next five years, if final feasibility and viability studies are positive. The total cost of these and related developments will be close to $265 million. The new Donkin mine will add about 1,200 jobs in industrial Cape Breton. Instead of the extremely poor condition of the mines prior to Devco, while we are not without problems, this government is proud that Devco miners and management have developed the Lingan mine into one of the most efficient, perhaps the most efficient, long wall coal mine in the world.
In an age when it is claimed people do not want to work, Devco management and miners volunteered by the hundreds to go down five miles of tunnels out under the ocean to fight a fire in No. 26 mine several years ago. Why? Because they wanted to save their mine and their jobs.
What began as a welfare operation is transforming itself into a viable, proud industry. That is a result of the regional development policies of this government. There is work still to be done before the caterpillar becomes a butterfly, but we on this side know it will succeed. We know Cape Bretoners can do it, and we will support their efforts.
We stand now on the brink of over $265 million worth of new development in the coal industry. We got here not because someone said you should do this and that, but because DREE, working hand in hand with the province of Nova Scotia and Devco, found the coal reserves to make a new mine and to make the rehabilitation of No. 26 mine possible. These accomplishments are not accidents. They are the result of foresight, planning, hard work, co-operation within the federal government, and co-operation with the province of Nova Scotia. This government delivers. Also I refer to Devco's bed and breakfast program in tourism, Devco's revitalizing of sheep farming operations, Devco's oyster farming development, Devco's trout development, and many other things in which it has been engaged. Devco has a new president, Mr. Bob Matheson. Personally I have full confidence in him. He is competent, and I am sure he will lead Devco to more successes.

speechtext: Which constituency is he running in?

speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
