speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that Mr. Matheson is not in the race. He heads Devco. He comes from Cape Breton. He is the son of a miner who has made a career as a lawyer, just as my hon. colleague of the opposition, and who wants to take up the challenge of contributing to revive the economy of the area where he was born and where he grew up. Mr. Speaker, I could go on, but I see that you are about to interrupt me so I will close by saying that the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is an excellent one, that it has been well received by the general public and that it will certainly win the support of the majority of members of the House when the question will be put for the last time, and I wish to thank him.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not participated in too many budget debates in the past, but I am privileged to do so on this occasion. The single item in this budget rated by most people as being the most important was the provincial governments' involvement in their provincial sales tax reductions. Certainly it has provided most of the after-budget news commentary and comments in this parliament.
However, the single item which appealed to me was the inclusion of an amendment to the capital gains tax law that provides for the deferral of capital gains in intergenerational

April 20, 1978

transfers of family farms and partnerships. I am sure hon. members on both sides of this chamber will recall that I was somewhat enthusiastic over this specific item in the budget. Perhaps they will recall also that this same item provoked the greatest spontaneous applause in the House over any other budget item. It marked the successful culmination of over five years of persistent, personal effort, commencing in 1973 with Mr. Turner, followed by Mr. Macdonald, and finally by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien).
In retrospect, this change in the capital gains tax laws had to come, or we would have seen the end of our family farm and ranch way of life due to the ravages of seven years of galloping land inflation and the availability of foreign capital. In any event, I thank the hon. Minister of Finance and his policy advisers for this particular budget item. I know of many long-established family cattle ranch units which would join me in expressing this appreciation to the minister. I hope that his parliamentary secretary will convey that personal message to the minister. I am sure that the minister and his parliamentary secretary will understand when I suggest quite seriously that I feel that I can take considerable credit for this tax change in this budget.
I would like now to make some remarks about various energy aspects of the budget, in particular respecting remarks made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) in this debate on April 13. The minister was speaking about a Canadian strategy to establish an energy policy, and he had pointed out that it had three basic elements. The third element was of interest to me, which "was to develop our own indigenous supplies of oil, particularly the non-conventional sources-the tar sands and the heavy oils of western Canada." I mention this reference to draw attention to a new source of heavy crude that exists now in my Medicine Hat constituency, and that is on the Suffield military reserve.
I am sure members are aware that there is now substantial production of natural gas from this field. It is being produced by the Alberta Energy Company that is owned almost totally by the people of Alberta. This Suffield gas production will increase steadily as the present drilling program continues. What is not generally known is that heavy crude is also being produced in modest quantities in that same Suffield area, and there are now about 30 heavy crude wells in various stages of drilling and production.
Heavy crude oil, of course, is more expensive to produce and is priced below conventional oils. Thus there is a very valid reason for that extra world price provision provided for in Bill C-19, which is the Petroleum Administration Act that was passed last Monday night.
At the end of that debate I made a short intervention in support of the inclusion of these Suffield heavy crudes in the group of heavy crudes that will enjoy these higher world prices. The Minister of Finance has recognized the need for heavy crude production in this budget by extending the manufacturing and processing tax incentive to upgrade heavy oil.
The Budget-Mr. Hargrave
This does not include plants established in relation to bituminous sand mining projects. This incentive in the budget should apply to the Suffield heavy crudes.
The economics of producing both gas and oil at the shallow Suffield depth can be appreciated from a comparison of average drilling costs in western Canada to offshore costs based on 1976 figures. These comparisons were recently published in the bulletin entitled "Energy Update 1977" which was put out by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. I wish to give a few quotations from pages 13 and 14 of that bulletin. On page 13 it says:
The combination of higher well-head prices and provincial drilling incentives resulted in a dramatic increase in exploration spending in western Canada. This drilling activity paid off in a significant expansion of our gas reserves as 80 per cent of the record 6,300 wells drilled were for natural gas exploration and development.
Additions to our natural gas reserves from shallow producing horizons such as those found in the Suffield Block in southeastern Alberta have been well ahead of the annual consumption rate. These drilling successes have spurred additional programs across the prairies.
I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that this very positive comment is mainly due to Alberta's excellent incentive policies.
There is an interesting table of costs listed in this same bulletin on page 14, which is headed "Average Drilling Costs in Western Canada and Offshore, 1976" and gives the costs of four locations, Alberta; other western provinces; Northwest Territories, Yukon and the Arctic, and the fourth one, east coast offshore. I would like to quote two costs. One is the cost per total foot and the other is the cost per total well. First of all, the cost per total foot: Alberta $33.98; other western provinces $57.16; Northwest Territories, Yukon and the Arctic $770.70, and east coast offshore, $243.14.
Going to cost per total well, we get into the big money: in Alberta again, $108,129; other western provinces $283,482; in the Northwest Territories, Yukon, and Arctic $7,848,444. And on the east cost offshore, $4,818,200. It should be noted that these are actual total costs per producing well and do not include development and exploratory costs, which are usually much higher.
It will surprise no one in this chamber that I want to make a few comments about our Canadian cattle industry. I want to make a brief review of the financial side of our total Canadian beef cattle industry, and I want to say quickly that that side is certainly not the panacea that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) suggested in his budget speech a couple of days ago. In my opinion, the last three years-1975, 1976 and 1977-have been the most difficult years in the modern history of our cattle industry, and that includes the 1930's. This is about a 40-year period.
The single worst year was 1976. This is in relevant terms, of course, in relating market prices to production costs. Probably the most factual record and research in this critical three year phase of Canada's cattle industry is contained in a recent publication entitled "Economic Research Report", and it goes on in the title with a little more detail, "An Analysis of the Costs and Returns in the Canadian Beef Industry, 1970-

April 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Hargrave
1977" rep0rt was pUt out by a firm named Broadwith, Hughes and Associates Ltd. of Guelph, Ontario, and was dated September, 1977. This report was completed at the request of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association.
One of the authors, Mr. David Hughes, was a former senior staff officer of the Food Prices Review Board. I would like to give some very significant quotations from the chapter entitled "Summary and Conclusions":
-aggregate net income in Canadian feedlot operations showed generally increasing returns between 1970 and 1973 with 1971 and 1973 being exceptionally good years. A dramatic reversal of fortunes occurred in 1974 when net income fell from plus $77 million in 1973 to minus $46 million in 1974. A partial recovery was experienced in 1975 but a further dramatic fall in net income occurred in 1976 from a position of plus $19 million in 1975 to minus $84 million in 1976 ...
Western cattle feeders appear to have had a comparative advantage in feeding cattle over their eastern counterparts during the 1970 to 1973 period. However, relatively greater increases in feed costs in the west in 1974 and 1975 completely eroded this advantage in those years.
It goes on as follows:
Net income returns to Canadian cow/calf operations showed a similar increasing aggregate net income picture to the feedlot sector over the period 1970 to 1973 but experienced an equally dramatic change in fortunes in 1974 when the net income level fell well below those achieved between 1970 and 1973. The decline in aggregate net income in the cow/calf sector has been sustained through 1975 and 1976. Net income has moved from a positive of plus $390 million or plus $78 per cow in 1973 to a position of minus $246 million or minus $40 per cow in 1976. It is interesting to note that the full impact of depressed prices for slaughter cattle were not felt until 1975 or 1976 in the cow/calf sector and that the size of the Canadian beef cow herd was still increasing in 1975.
On the next page appears the following short sentence:
In summary the dramatic change in fortunes in the beef industry in 1974 resulted from a coincidental sharp decline in slaughter cattle prices and a sharp increase in feed costs.
Later there occurs this sentence:
The most startling revelation of the analysis is the dramatic changes in net income returns from quarter to quarter and from period to period in the feedlot sector and to a certain extent the cow/calf sector.
Later on the report states:
As an adjunct to this it seems incongruous to us that the beef cow herd in Canada was still increasing in 1975, given that industry signals of impending losses in the industry were apparent in early 1974.
I remind hon. members that the decline in the cattle herd actually started in September, 1975. Mr. Speaker, that concludes the quotations from that interesting analysis of the difficult period from which we have just emerged.
The report clearly identifies a total Canadian industry loss in equity over the last three and one-half years of over $400 million. What this very factual report does not comment on or identify are the deep scars that are now apparent in our cattle industry. Many cattle producers, particularly young cattlemen, and perhaps some of those who got into the exotic side of the industry, are no longer with us. In the United States it is estimated that 200,000 cattlemen are no longer in the industry-that is 13 per cent of their producers. There are no comparable figures that I am aware of for Canada. At the usual ratio of 1 to 10, however, we could have 20,000 less cattle producers in Canada today.

In addition to these scars, there are other significant changes in our cattle and beef industry and in beef consumer preferences. It was the liquidation phase of the cattle cycle beginning in September, 1975, that saw a 15 per cent drop in cow numbers in both Canada and United States; it was this liquidation phase that spawned the present hamburger craze. In 1977, 54 per cent of beef eaten in the United States was in the form of hamburger. The Canadian figure is probably just a little lower. Now that the big cow selldown is over in both countries, consumers will probably not want to return to the much higher percentage of choice steaks and roasts of former years because our society has become accustomed to and is satisfied with the fast food service so readily available on the North American continent. This is a logical and progressive development in our beef eating habits which should bring fed cattle prices and non-fed cattle prices, that is, cows and grass cattle, closer together. Fed cattle prices would come down and non-fed cattle prices would probably move up. This would be good for both the cattle industry and for consumers.
Most important of all, however, in the industry's recovery process from those three years of disaster, is the deep concern of cattlemen that our industry will have the opportunity to recoup that $400 million odd equity loss through the market place.
Over the last two months our North American cattle and beef markets have clearly strengthened, and strengthened rather quickly. Our industry can recover through the market place if the government allows our market system to function without political interference. It is only common cow sense that the good market price years have to carry the bad years.
Two days ago, during the rambling remarks of the Minister of Agriculture in this budget debate, he conveniently stuck to vague generalities instead of making at least a few specific comments about such things as his beef import law that we used to hear about. It now seems obvious that the great competition between this minister and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) about who would sponsor this new legislation has been called off completely and replaced by that very deliberately vague joint statement on March 30, indicating that the Export and Import Permits Act would continue to set quotas, but only for the next three years. These quotas, they pointed out, are to be based upon the base period of 1971-1975.
There was a very interesting phrase in that statement of March 30 which referred to those quotas. The phrase "adjusted for changes in domestic beef consumption since this base period" referred to the quotas that could be set under the Export and Import Permits Act. Canadian beef consumption for the base period 1971-75 was approximately 94 pounds per capita; last year we probably ate about 113 pounds per capita, and the estimate for 1979 is 95 pounds per capita. There are indications that our Canadian cow numbers are already too low to produce the ideal domestic supply of between 90 and 100 pounds per capita. We know, for example, that the next cattle cycle will peak approximately in 1985. Today, our industry has already determined the beef supply, that is, our
April 20, 1978

domestic beef supply for 1980 and 1981. It is here now, on the ground.
Our producer concern is, quite bluntly, that this vague phrase "adjusted for changes in domestic beef consumption since this base period" could be interpreted by the two ministers as an appropriate excuse to increase those offshore beef quotas-perhaps even this year but certainly over the next three years. Surely our Minister of Agriculture would not stoop so low, but it is a matter of concern. This is the reason cattlemen will continue to insist on a Canadian beef import law that would establish the rules by legislation and not be subject to change by this minister, future ministers of agriculture, or orders in council.
Another specific item that the Minister of Agriculture might have remarked upon-perhaps it was deliberately omitted-is the matter of a possible fed cattle payout for the first quarter of 1977. Both the minister and his staff have deliberately teased us with hints that there may be one, depending on what percentage figure, 90 or 95 per cent, is to be used. Now, almost 13 months after that period has ended with no final statement being made, we can only assume that this payout depends not on the stabilization legislation but on how much money the minister can get from Treasury and the political advantage he can get from a late announcement just before the election.
I must say I find it regrettable that the minister's original concept of stabilization with its stop loss approach seems to have all but disappeared. It has disappeared in favour of a cost of production index approach which is never explained or divulged, and the minister's power of discretion in varying that percentage figure used. We have already seen a percentage figure of 90, 95, 100; and in one instance up to 105 per cent.
There are some very obvious lessons which all of us, cattlemen and politicians, should have learned from this critical three- to four-year crisis from which our Canadian cattle industry has just emerged.
First of all it is appropriate to point out that in 1972 our Canadian Cattleman's Association in a beef seminar warned of an over-supply situation from a too rapid cow build-up, which continued to its peak in 1975. As a producers' organization we warned back in 1972 that that situation would surely develop, and it came about just as we predicted. However, no one, especially governments, listened to us at that time.
Today, when we are on the up side of the market price cycle, I want to remind all concerned that the Canadian Cattleman's Association has initiated a new "Beef Watch" policy to try to anticipate the cattle and beef cycle and then to project trends and advise accordingly. Some encouragement and attention to this new approach by cattle producers themselves are surely warranted, especially by consumers and governments.
Finally, there is no question that our Canadian cattle industry has survived perhaps the most difficult price-cost phase in our history, but at a cost which we do not yet really know. That $400 million figure which I pointed out is the actual cash
The Budget-Mr. Cullen
cost as near as anyone can find, but there is much more of a cost than that.
In the west the drought, and the severe winter which is only now just over, have added to that cost, especially across southern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan. Hopefully we, as producers, and particularly politicians, will learn from this experience. I sincerely hope so.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to follow the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave). Debates in this House are improved when we hear from him and from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) on a significant part of the agricultural community. It is a little unfair from the standpoint of the Minister of Agriculture because he has to cover the whole spectrum of agriculture in Canada and could not deal in a specific way with all of the items which the member for Medicine Hat suggests. I know that his speech will be very carefully read by the minister and he will call out that which should be taken.
In addition to being Minister of Employment and Immigration for Canada, it is also my privilege to be the member of parliament for Sarnia-Lambton. On behalf of my constituents I want to say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) that the budget was very well received in my region of the country. I listened to a radio broadcast from Ottawa on that particular night, I believe it was radio station CKOY, and its business consultant said that the senior citizens of Canada should stand up and cheer at the announcement made by the Minister of Finance in connection with the registered retirement savings plans, the options which are available to senior citizens, and the Registered Retirement Investment Fund referred to in the budget.
I think it is an appropriate move made by the minister so that senior citizens will now have a better opportunity to deal with the money which they have saved over the years, and still maintain the basic principle of the RRSP, which is, after all, meant to be retirement income.
The large concession made regarding research and development will sit well with the petrochemical industry in my area.
The sales tax cuts have won unanimous approval from citizens across the country, not only in my riding. We have heard some criticism of the fact that this was an invasion of provincial rights, or that it was not the appropriate way to deal with it. When one looks at the number of meetings and the number of times which the Minister of Finance travelled across Canada and met with the ministers of finance of the various provinces, on a multilateral and bilateral basis always bearing in mind the concern about secrecy respecting the budget, as there should be, I think we have to adopt a little bit more of a practical approach. In the final analysis the decision taken was adopted by nine out of the ten provinces of this country.
Certainly it is right that maybe we should be looking at other avenues of approach such as specific types of sales tax, and in this particular way we can work in conjunction with the

April 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Cullen
provinces. But most assuredly we must applaud the Minister of Finance for being able to meet with his provincial counterparts and come up with a program which is acceptable to nine out of the ten provinces.
In Lambton County, my riding, which was the former historic riding of Lambton West, there is a large rural element. All of us who have concern for people in that particular region, and I have some knowledge of that having spent some 12 years as solicitor for the County of Lambton, welcome the fact that the Minister of Finance saw fit to deal with incorporated farms and allow them to move from one generation to another without penalty of taxation. I think that move was appropriate. Obviously there was concern by the Minister of Finance that it might set some kind of precedent for other small businesses and the like. He took this step forward and I think it was an appropriate one, given the contribution that the primary producer makes to the people of Canada. Whoever deserves the credit, Mr. Speaker, in the final analysis the time must be chosen and the amount of money must be found so that this particular move can be made. It was a very grave move considering all of the other pressures that were being brought to bear at that particular time.
There is a genuine, legitimate concern by all members of this House, whatever their political persuasion, about the level of unemployment in Canada. Fortunately this government's employment measures, carried out on a significant scale, are geared to stimulating the economy without rekindling inflation and, most important, are targeted to groups in areas of the country particularly hard hit by unemployment. This is especially so, of course, in the case of direct job creation.
Over the past ten years, the Canadian labour force has increased by almost three million people, some 37 per cent. In total, some 2.3 million more people were employed in 1977 than ten years ago. But the continuing population growth and the continued influx of new entrants into the labour force have contributed to the present high levels of unemployment.
Unfortunately for the Canadian public, and in dealing with the problem of unemployment, the opposition parties' response has been poorly researched, sometimes reprehensible and on most occasions it will not work, at least it will not work as claimed by the opposition parties.
The misrepresentations and distortions perpetuated by a number of members of the opposition have contributed to a serious misunderstanding not only of the nature of the unemployment in Canada but also of the scope and the rationale of the government's programs to combat unemployment.
The comments of the members of the NDP have been singularly inaccurate. Their spokesman even has a hard time reading statistics correctly. It is a fact that Statistics Canada, and they use Statistics Canada, has estimated the actual numbers of unemployed in March, 1978, to have averaged one million. Admittedly, this number is higher than any of us would like to see, and the matter is of great concern. Nonetheless, the NDP insists on distorting these figures arbitrarily by adding over 600,000 individuals and referring to the over 1.6 million unemployed Canadians, an exaggeration of some 60

per cent. Furthermore, it attempts to rationalize these irresponsible statements by alleging that the difference of 600,000 is made up of discouraged workers, when the facts produced by Statistics Canada indicate that only 64,000 individuals in March could legitimately be classified as such. Even after making allowances for this, one can readily see that the NDP exaggerates the unemployment rate by some 50 per cent over the true figure. It is a very small example of the loose way in which that party bandies statistics around to suit its own purposes.
The trumped-up analysis of the opposition does not stop with misstatements about the labour market. It also includes concoctions with respect to the impact of recent changes in the unemployment insurance program on the labour market. A number of municipalities have recently experienced increases in their social assistance case loads. This situation has led to a number of unfounded allegations about the extent to which recent legislative changes to the unemployment insurance program have been responsible for those increases.
These allegations have been based upon data deliberately selected out of context, and this has left a misleading impression as to the potential impact of unemployment insurance on social assistance case loads. The allegations have been based on data from a few municipalities relating to only a small portion of social welfare recipients who are defined as "employable". In fact, no consistent data or definitions of types of persons on welfare exist across provinces, and the statistical evidence cited to support these allegations is totally misleading.
In fact, those increases in social assistance which have occured are primarily the result of slack economic conditions. In these circumstances many Canadians are having difficulty in finding or maintaining jobs. This has resulted in large and continuing increases in unemployment insurance benefit expenditures. However, it has never been intended that the unemployment insurance program should act as a total and eternal security blanket for all Canadian workers. Responsibility for income maintenance is divided among a variety of programs and jurisdictions.
I suspect, Mr. Speaker, that the opposition knows all too well the real facts about the employment picture, but that it is to their advantage either to distort them or ignore them altogether. In doing so, they deliberately rob people of hope. Let me put before you the true employment picture.
From 1970 to 1976, the latest period for which international comparisons are available, the number of Canadian jobs actually increased by 21 per cent, double that of the United States, which recorded the next largest increase of 11 per cent in the same period. France and Japan experienced a growth of only 5 per cent and 4 per cent respectively, and Germany's work force actually declined by 2.5 per cent. No other country has been as successful in meeting the challenge of providing additional employment opportunities for such a rapidly growing labour force.
April 20, 1978

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Regardless of these facts, the opposition still speaks of unemployment as if we were back in the thirties. Although the unemployment rate is high and, indeed, too high, it can no longer be regarded in the same light as that of a generation ago when the unemployment rate was rising due to numbers of jobs decreasing rather than numbers of workers increasing. A case in point: over the past 12 months, although the Canadian economy created some 330,000 jobs, some 432,000 workers entered the labour force.
This is a phenomenal increase in the number of people actually working in the course of a year. The fact that we have something like 62.4 per cent of people in the labour force as compared to 50 per cent many years ago, in the sixties and thirties, indicates where our problem is.
In any job creation we attempt, we cannot keep up with the numbers of people entering the work force. For instance, it has resulted in a situation in which there is a significant number of families with multiple earners. In fact, almost two thirds of the unemployed are in families with at least one other wage earner, so that the families are not altogether without income. I would not want to suggest that these additional sources of income are unimportant, or not required. But I do suggest that unemployment no longer means what it used to mean: a complete loss of all family income with resultant hardship and despair.
The Minister of Agriculture stated in his address the other night that to make a comparison with the thirties is absolutely ludicrous, considering at that time there was no unemployment insurance, no mobility grants, no training allowance and, in fact, no medicare. To compare unemployment and the unemployed person today with the thirties is not kosher, which is as charitable a word as I can think of.
There is no doubt that this still adds up to a situation where unemployment is at a level considerably higher than we would like it to be, and the Government of Canada shares the responsibility with the provinces and with the private sector to move to alleviate this problem. To some members of the opposition parties, the solution is simple, "spend our way out of it". Let us turn for a moment to some of the official opposition's proposals.
Personally, I looked forward with some expectation to the results of the three-member task force of the official opposition, about how they would cope with the unemployment situation. To be as charitable as I can, Mr. Speaker, I found the report pathetic. Someone referred to it as so much warmed over soup. The Conservative opposition sent three hand-wringers across the country and, after a great press release, much hyperbole, obviously altogether too much rhetoric, the pusillanimous result has been embarrassing to the official opposition, to the extent that they hoped that any press comment on it would be buried on page ten. One of their more ridiculous proposals tells how they would solve the problem of university graduates by putting them into debt or further into debt by lending them unemployment insurance benefits for a period of
The Budget-Mr. Cullen
time, which benefits would have to be, of course, paid back later and so, I assume, would the premiums. Hardly adequate, Mr. Speaker. One might equally argue that fire insurance can be purchased after the fire! I very much doubt that those employees and employers who are currently paying premiums and who share the risk of benefit costs would accept this proposal to create a special class of citizens who would be exempt from the rules which apply to everyone else.
The NDP proposed measures to prevent unemployment would involve the launching of programs whose impact is highly questionable. In particular, I refer to the NDP proposal to launch $400 million for a municipal capital works program, on the misguided assumption that it would create some 60,000 new jobs. Indeed, one common and irresponsible feature of the NDP employment proposals is the completely unrealistic and inflated estimates of the number of additional jobs they would create. Note, Mr. Speaker, I said additional jobs.
Our experience with a capital works program in the municipalities in 1971 convinced us that this was not the most effective way of creating additional employment. That was a Liberal party program. If we thought it had done the job suggested for it by the NDP, we would have implemented it at the present time. We would have been great heroes with all the municipalities. We would have been perpetrating a fraud by suggesting to those who want to work that this program would creat 60,000 new jobs when we knew, after studying what we had done, that that program just does not work in that way. Having said that, we say there are other programs. The NDP will not lend us one iota of support for any innovative approach that we suggest.
The irony of it all, and one has only to pick up Hansard on any day this House is sitting for proof of what I am saying, is that the opposition is continuously assaulting this government. The fact of the matter is that whenever this government does come up with new and innovative approaches, the opposition's attitude has constantly been to shoot them down on sight and dismiss them out of hand. Let me point out one instance, Mr. Speaker, when the government has been able to overcome the critics of the opposition and implement, after countless hours of arguing and debating, what may well turn out to be the innovation of the decade in changing conditions in our labour market. I am talking about the developmental use of unemployment insurance funds, which was bitterly opposed by members of the opposition during consideration of Bill C-27.
Work sharing was the subject of particular opposition attack. This is what the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), had to say in the House of Commons on June 23, 1977, about the developmental use of unemployment insurance funds for work sharing:
One of the so-called progressive ideas offered in this bill is work-sharing. That was very prevalent in the days of the depression. It is not a creative approach to employment, and the government knows it.
For his part, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) concluded, and I quote:
-organized labour and indeed the industrial community do not look with any great amount of favour or interest upon this proposal. It is somewhat useless for

April 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Cullen
the government to say this is a part of a new employment strategy, if in fact there is little interest or co-operation on the horizon from these significant groups.
However, even now, before we have envisaged embarking on pilot projects, initiatives have been and are being taken by workers and employers to establish work-sharing arrangements. As a result, we have already launched 14 work-sharing agreements in which approximately 1,900 workers have participated or are participating in. To date, the lay-offs of nearly 770 individuals have been averted. Companies, supported fully by their employees, have approached us in such numbers that the pilot phase of the program is very heavily booked. Whatever the results of these pilot programs, they will certainly not fail from lack of interest on the part of employers or employees. If we had listened to the members of the opposition, these, and undoubtedly other individuals in the future, would be on our unemployment rolls instead of actively working.
Again, if we had heeded the NDP, we would not have pressed forward with the developmental use of UI funds for training. But, by introducing this feature, we managed to free up some $42 million in 1978/79 to provide full-time training for an additional 17,500 Canadians in areas and occupations where unemployment needs can be identified. The total number of Canadians in full-time training will now be approximately 234,000 in 1978/79.
The government's employment measures are vigorous ones. While the government has moved to stimulate the economy, it has had to recognize that the serious danger of inflation remains with us and that expansionary measures must take account of this reality. Consequently, we have adopted a series of specific programs and activities designed to alleviate or reduce unemployment. However, it seems that whenever I speak of my department's programs, like Canada Works and Young Canada Works, the opposition quickly dismisses them as insignificant and trivial. Let the opposition tell this to the more than 185,000 individuals who got a job in 1977/78 because of employment measures brought in by this government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The following are among the government's recent measures designed to stimulate the economy and alleviate unemployment-some $1.2 billion dollars have been allocated for the two fiscal years ending in 1979. These include $458 million for the employment strategy for the fiscal years 1977/78 and 1978/79, including $50 million allocated to the new economic growth component of Canada Works to stimulate growth in the private sector; $150 million for the federal labour intensive program; $200 million allocated to the new employment tax credit program for this year and next. It is expected that this will result in 100,000 new jobs. In addition, there are the clear employment-creating effects of the recent
budget in the area of sales tax reductions which it is expected will directly yield 25,000 new jobs.
Given the magnitude and complexity of our unemployment problems and our budgetary constraints, there are limits to the extent to which we can allocate additional financial resources to our labour market programs. In these circumstances, we simply cannot afford the option of buying our way out of difficulties. Government spending on job creation must be kept in careful balance, in order not to increase inflationary pressure which would eventually result in even higher levels of unemployment. Prime Minister James Callaghan of Great Britain expressed what I consider a tremendously logical view of this problem. Remember, he is a member of the Labour Party-in this country he might be in the NDP. The only difference is that he happens to be in power and that he happens to accept responsibility for fiscal measures. This is what he said:
We used to think that you could spend your way out of recession and increase employment by cutting taxes and boosting government spending. I tell you, in all candor, that that option no longer exists and that insofar as it ever did exist, it only worked by injecting bigger doses of inflation into the economy followed by higher levels of unemployment as the next stop.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then why did they reduce taxes by two billion pounds?

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would never in my wildest dreams try to determine what the Labour Party might do in Britain. But here is a Labour Prime Minister who has stated that that policy does not work.
The measures introduced by the Minister of Finance in his budget are designed to stimulate the economy in such a manner that we will achieve our projected targets of real growth while, at the same time, have a minimum effect in stimulating inflation. Economic growth is, of course, in the long run the answer to our problems in the labour market. These problems are not going to be fully resolved this month or this year. But those who predict nothing but doom and gloom are not facing the facts. As I have said, our major cause of unemployment is not our inability to create jobs-during the past 12 months the economy generated no less than 330,000 new jobs. Our problem is that the labour force has grown with such great speed, and for so long a period.
But that growth is unlikely to continue into the indefinite future. A few years from now, it is entirely likely that growth rates will be far less than our present 21 per cent, and new entrants to the labour force will have far less difficulty in finding jobs. What we have to do now-and I submit what we are doing now-is to maintain a reasonable pattern of steady economic growth, backed up by a sound program of job creation and training. Supplemented by an effective placement service and supported by a comprehensive income-maintenance program, we will remain one of the most prosperous and economically healthy countries of the western world.
[Mr. Cullen.)
April 20, 1978

It is nice to be able to rise in this chamber today. A few days ago we thought we might be away from Parliament Hill at this
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
time, taking our case to the people. That is what seemed likely after the Prime Minister's performance last Monday when he stamped out of the House in a well acted fit of pique which followed a familiar pattern. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) cannot answer a question, he aggravates the opposition into heckling him and then, when he is heckled, he claims he cannot be heard because of the heckling and he walks out. On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) raised a point of order with regard to a statement I made concerning the recommendations contained in a report to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). So that there might be no doubt as to the words which were used, I will read the recommendation, which is as follows:
A special unemployment benefit should be established for university students entering the labour force in areas where the unemployment rate exceeds the national average. During a three year trial period, new workers would be able to receive benefits equalling the average benefit of their province for up to six months. The premiums necessary to establish a benefit period would be paid after employment had been found.
That is a reimbursement of the premiums, as I have indicated. They are moving students into further areas of debts, and this is inconsistent with the universality of the program and inconsistent with the people who are already contributing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not often that we have an example, which the minister has demonstrated, of the arrogance of this government. The minister seems to feel justified in interrupting other members' speeches to go back to previous speeches.
Right now what we are concerned about is Canada's situation. I should like to read a few words from the New York Times of Sunday, April 16, in the days following our budget. It is headed "Canada and Britain Unveil Budgets". It reads:
Significant steps to faster growth in two of the world's weakest economies were taken last week as Canada and Britain announced their budgets for the coming year.
How does it feel after ten years to be one of the world's weakest economies? Are you members opposite proud of your record? The article goes on to read:
Of the two, Canada's program is more stimulative, reflecting the more serious economic problems facing that country.
I guess that makes us the worst in the world. The article goes on to read:
The budget of the Canadian government calls for record spending of $46.9 billion in the fiscal year that began April 1, with a deficit of $11.5 billion-by far the largest in Canada's history ... Judging from first reactions, however, the Canadian public is skeptical as to whether all this can do much to combat their nation's persistent unemployment-

April 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
Which is, incidentally, the responsibility of the department of the minister who has just spoken. The article goes on to read:
-now at a post-depression high of 9.7 per cent. S. F. Hughes, executive director of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, was wary lest temporary treatment be followed by new headaches.
You will recall that Mr. Hughes, at least in the five years that I have been listening to these budgets, has approved of every one of them, to my recollection. He always thinks they are good budgets that will improve things. If any member opposite can tell me of any budget in the last six years that has put the economy at the time of the next budget in a better state than it was in, I would like to hear it.
The article goes on to read:
The budget proposals, he said, "may only serve to encourage consumer spending in the shorter term, at the expense of 1979".
But by then, I guess, the election will be over. The article goes on to read:
Worse, many observers fear that Canada's budgetary stimulus, combined with the imminent lifting of the strict wage and price controls imposed at the end of 1975, could lead to a new wave of inflation. As if in anticipation, the value of the Canadian dollar slipped to a 45 year low of 87 U.S. cents after the budget was announced. Only 18 months ago the Canadian was worth $1.03 in American currency.
In Britain, the mood is far more optimistic.
That is as close as we can get to an objective viewpoint of our economy if we go to other countries and read what their papers, which have no axe to grind, have to say about it.
It seems to me that the question is one of tax rates and of tax revenue. I have been reading an interesting book which deals with a system of a university professor in California, Professor Laffer. Professor Laffer is a very intelligent man. There are two rates of taxation at which the revenue is zero. If you charge zero tax, then the revenue will be zero; if you charge 100 per cent tax, the revenue will also be zero because nobody will produce anything. There is a variable point at which revenues and production are at their maximum. If you can find that point, then you will have an economy that is high in production and high in revenue. The location depends largely, strangely enough, on the wishes of the people, a point which is often missed by politicians and by governments which seem more interested in maximum revenues.
During wars, for example, taxes can be very high, without losing productivity, and revenues will be high. When the war ends, the people no longer want massive government interference or provision of arms and services. They want to be taxed at a lower rate. History shows that the results of lowering taxes can increase revenues. This is the point that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) was making in his speech on the budget.
I will give you a few historic examples. In the United States there was a recession in 1919 to 1920 when they were operating under the philosophy that wartime taxes should be left high, ostensibly to pay off the massive debts they had incurred during World War I. Warren Harding, who was not the world's greatest president, was elected in a landslide on a
(Mr. McKinnon.]
"return to normalcy" platform, and the subsequent cut in taxes led to the prosperity of the 1920's.
After World War II the Americans, who had learned the lesson from World War I, reduced taxes immediately and had a prosperous transition to the post-war period. Japan and Germany left their taxes high for the first few years, and stagnated. In 1948 Ludwig Erhard lowered taxes and the German recovery began. In 1950 Japan reduced taxes, and her economic recovery is now history. Reduced taxes increased their productivity and revenues.
I should like to read a short quote from The Public Interest about taxes, revenues and the "Laffer curve". It reads:
Andrew Mellon became a national hero for engineering the rate reductions of the 1920's, and was called "the greatest treasury secretary since Alexander Hamilton". The financial policies of Ludwig Erhard were responsible for what was hailed as "an economic miracle"-the post-war recovery of Germany. Throughout history, however, it has been the exception rather than the rule that politicians, by accident or design, have sought to increase revenues by lowering rates.
Finally, we should note that in 1962-1964 under John F. Kennedy, the U.S. cut taxes sharply and the U.S. economy promptly expanded and produced more revenues. What I am saying is that the recommendations, spelled out by the Leader of the Opposition earlier in this debate, for important tax cuts have a sound basis and have been proven successful in many countries in the modern era. Income tax directly affects the incentive to work.
I have one more quote out of The Public Interest. It reads:
The idea behind the "Laffer curve" is no doubt as old as civilization, but unfortunately politicians have always had trouble grasping it. In his essay, Of Taxes, written in 1756, David Hume pondered the problem:
"Exorbitant taxes, like extreme necessity, destroy industry by producing despair; and even before they reach this pitch, they raise the wages of the labourer and manufacturer, and heighten the price of all commodities.
David Hume knew that in 1756, but this government does not know it yet.
Now I would like to go to the second part of my speech which is on defence, the area for which I am responsible to the Leader of the Opposition. I would like to point out that if defence is ever to be discussed or spoken of in the House, it is up to the opposition to do it. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) is following what is getting to be a short tradition, established by his predecessor, of practically never speaking on defence in the House of Commons. We have had the new minister for a year and a half, during which time he has not spoken to the House on defence, except in answer to questions. It is a government that will not speak publicly about defence, and it falls upon us in the opposition to do the job for them. This is a sorry state of affairs in itself.
What is the state of Canadian defence? What is the state of our alliances? Alliances constitute the framework of Canada's defence policy, that is, NATO and NORAD. Let me turn first to our problems with our NATO policy. Recently the Minister of National Defence woke up to the difficulties inherent in our reinforcement roles to the northern flank of NATO, that is, Norway. We have had this commitment since 1968, but neither he nor his predecessor noticed the problem before,
April 20, 1978

despite the fact we were constantly reminding him of it. We understand now that the minister on his trip to Norway was talking over the reinforcement of the northern flank to which we were committed, and he found he had to ask for Norwegian naval assistance to convoy our troops.
Let no one be surprised that we have had to ask for help. In the last eight years we have managed to raise federal spending from $16 billion to $46 billion without finding enough money to lay down the keel of one new ship. No new ship in the equipment replacement program will be ready for service before 1985 at the earliest. If we start moving right now to get those six frigates for the Canadian navy, they will not be here until 1985 at the earliest, and by then our fleet will be composed of venerable antiques.
The new program will produce six frigates by 1989. At that time there will be only four ships under 25 years of age, plus the six frigates, for a total of ten ships. At the present time we have 23 ships. This is the type of hard knocks one receives because of the program the government has followed for so many years. The government has not given any increases in the capital budget of the Department of National Defence.
I should like to refer to the age of Canadian ships. We have heard about the program of the Minister of National Defence via press releases. In answer to questions he indicated that six frigates would be built, and that they will be completed by 1989. At that time we will have our four DDH 280s. They will be 16, 17, 17, and 17 years of age. By 1989 they will be getting fairly well on. Most countries think 20 years is the optimum life of a ship in the navy.
If one takes the life span of a ship and stretches it to 25 years, Canada will have two ships in the Annapolis class. They will be the Annapolis and the Nipigon, both 25 years of age.
In the Mackenzie class, we will have the Mackenzie at age 27, the Qu'Appelle at age 26, the Saskatchewan at age 26, and the Yukon at age 26. All the ships in the Restigouche class are in reserve already, but by 1989 the Chaudiere will be age
30,	the Columbia will be age 30 and the St. Croix will be age
31.	In the improved Restigouche class, there will be three ships: the Gatineau at age 30, the Kootenay at age 30, the Restigouche at age 31 and the Terra Nova at age 30.
Next is the St. Laurent class, which is the oldest of them all. Sometimes I feel parliament needs a new St. Laurent, speaking in a political sense. In the St. Laurent class there will be the Saguenay at age 33, the Skeena at age 32, the Ottawa at age 33, the Margaree at age 32, the Fraser at age 32 and the Assiniboine at age 33. There is no secret about this. The fact is that the government did nothing about the replacement of ships, and is now moving slowly to replace them. By the time the first six are built, we will have only four that will be less than 25 years of age, and those are the DDH 280s.
I do not have a great deal to say with regard to the army situation. The army procurement for this summer will be a Leopard I tank. As I mentioned before in the House, it would have been preferable to continue renting the Leopard I, which
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
we are renting at the present time from Germany, for another year or so, and then purchase the Leopard II, which will be improved vastly over the Leopard I. At the time I propounded the idea in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, I was told we would have to wait until well into the 1980's for the Leopard II, but my information is that the Leopard II will be in use by the German forces in 1980.
I should like to refer to the main differences between the Leopard I and the Leopard II. The Leopard II is armed with a 120 millimetre gun, instead of a 105 millimetre gun, and it has Chobham type armour. Thus, it will have a new gun and new armour. Unfortunately, Canada is purchasing a Leopard I with the old gun and the old armour. I suspect they will be the last models off the assembly line, thus we will have a tank which is not the newest within a year after purchase.
Now I should like to deal with our air force. We have a NATO and a NORAD commitment. We require new aircraft for both of them. The importance of the role in determining what aircraft should be purchased must be stressed. In no way am I satisfied that this is understood by the government. NORAD is the difficult aspect of this problem. The Voodoos, or the CF 101s, obviously need replacement, yet their role is not as clear as when they were acquired.
I should like to refer to a new book which was written by Dr. Cuthbertson. It is entitled, "Canadian Military Independence in the Age of the Superpowers." Those who are interested in Canada's military future might be well advised to read it. One does not have to accept Dr. Cuthbertson's recommendations, but certainly it is a well-researched book. Page 86 refers to NORAD and what the Americans are doing about it. It reads as follows:
The United States plans to reduce its present 405 interceptors to 212 F-106s by mid-1980 ...
A principal reason why NORAD was renewed in 1973 without amendment for only two years was United States uncertainty about the relevancy of anti-bomber defence to its strategic requirements. Once anti-bomber defence was declared strategically redundant, the United States moved as rapidly to reduce and re-organize its air defence system as it had previously moved to establish it.
Against this very uncertain background, Canada is moving forward to purchase $2.3 billion worth of new fighter aircraft. The planes fall into two price classes: over $20 million each or under $20 million each. In the over $20 million, one will find the Toronado, which is made by the Panavia consortium of Britain, Italy and Germany; the F-14 and the F-15, which are two American planes. The F-14 and the F-15 are worth over $20 million each. Generally they are said to be multi-role fighters, they can shoot anything out of the skies, they have long ranges and very, very sophisticated equipment. In the under $20 million, one will find the F-16, F-18A and F-18L, which are American planes. The F-16 is a single-seater and has a single engine, compared to the others which are two and two.
I find it easy to support an immediate purchase for the NATO role, which is a ground support role for our troops in Germany. The role is there. It must be supported. We know what the troops and the planes are doing. It is quite a different

April 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
role than the NORAD role. Perhaps a good case could be made in favour of the purchase of the more exotic fighters such as the F-14 and the F-15 for the NORAD role, or the Toronado; but the need for such a plane for this anti-bomber role has not been proven to me, nor to the public.
The Americans consider the anti-bomber role to be declining. In fact our second last minister of national defence said that it was declining. Approximately 20 years ago ministers of national defence indicated that the anti-bomber role was becoming less important. Yet this role is put forward as a reason for acquiring new aircraft in support of NORAD. The forces would be wiser to point out the need of aircraft to see-off intruders. We require sovereignty of our air space. When one refers to the scenario concerning the manned bombers which will come over Canada and bomb our cities, one soon runs into difficulties attempting to carry through that scenario to its illogical conclusion.
There are other problems regarding NORAD, such as the AWACS, which is the Airborne Warning and Control System plane. It is particularly with reference to North American Air Defence. Where does the government stand in this? For months we have been asking what Canada intends to do with the AWACS. Are we going to participate or not? We have heard from one source that we will spend $180 million, and from other sources we have heard that it will be $300 million. The price of these planes has risen astronomically in the last while. The cost which will be entailed is almost beyond belief. We have not planned to get into it, but we might.
A year ago last January we heard a very interesting presentation by the then vice-chief of the defence staff, Admiral Falls. At the present time he is the Chief of the Defence Staff. When he was speaking to the Conference of Defence Associations he presented a very interesting chart which showed where and when the money was to be spent. The tank was budgeted for first and then the long range patrol aircraft. The long range patrol aircraft were to be purchased at the same time as the tanks, which has been the case. That was to be followed by the new fighter aicraft, and then the ship replacement program. You could see from the chart that that was going to happen. However, when you consider the cost of the AWACS that might well be thrown in there, it changes the picture.
Quoting from the New York Times, April 14, 1978:
West Germany and the United States would bear the largest part of the cost if NATO decides to acquire the AWACS,-
That is the airborne warning and control system. The secretary for defence in the United States is quoted:
-Mr. Brown said. As now conceived, acquisition would involve 12 aircraft at a total cost of $2 billion-
You may recall that we thought that the cost of long range patrol aircraft was high at $1 billion for 18, but this is $2 billion for 12 aircraft.
-The price for each aircraft would be more than $120 million at present prices with support cost included, Mr. Brown said.

The charts of Admiral Falls showed us at the time three things of particular importance to be noted, and they should be recognized at this time. First, there is no provision for the airborne warning and control system, so if we get into AWACS more money would be needed. Secondly, the amount of money is based on an annual increase of 12 per cent in real terms in the capital budget. This was an introduction that was brought in by the former minister of national defence before he quit his portfolio in October, 1976. He had managed, however, to wring out of the cabinet an agreement that he would be allowed to increase the capital budget of the Department of National Defence by 12 per cent per annum on a real basis, that is, they would add the inflation costs in and then add 12 per cent to the capital budget.
The third thing to be remembered is that this acquisition plan of the Admiral was drawn up bearing that in mind, and at the present time no allowance has been made for the devaluation of the dollar. If we follow our plans at the present rate, even if our dollar stayed exactly where it is now, we would need an additional $125 million to make up the extra money to buy the more expensive American currency or German deutschmark.
I come now to the most disturbing news of all, to those interested in national defence in Canada. The government has broken its promise concerning the 12 per cent real growth in the capital budget. This year's estimates call for only an additional 2.8 per cent in real terms. Strangely enough, the Minister of National Defence cannot accept this. He hates to leave that wonderful speech where he said there would be 12 per cent each year. On March 21, 1978, in an External Affairs and National Defence Committee meeting, I asked Mr. Davies, who is the associate deputy minister of finance for DND:
Could Mr. Davis tell us exactly how much the percentage increased, the real growth percentage increased, in the capital budget this year after you had deducted the $60 million?
This $60 million offered by the Minister of National Defence to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) as an Easter present or something.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Davies. It is nice to talk to an objective person.
Strangely enough-there may be some logical answer for it, but it has certainly escaped me so far-on April 18 the Minister of National Defence was speaking at the committee meeting, and I quote from those minutes:
Well, first of all, the increase is one that was committed of 12 per cent increase per year plus the escalating factor on capital equipment.
This indicates that there is a bare-faced difference between what the associate deputy minister of finance for DND said and what the Minister of National Defence said at that time. I

April 20, 1978

presume that the minister will correct it at the first opportunity.
Perhaps the most blatant of the broken promises of the government as far as defence is concerned is this failure to provide funds for the formula announced by both this minister and his predecessor, that 12 per cent real growth in the capital budget. Let me say once again that the real growth for 1978-79 is only 2.8 per cent. This is going to have an exaggerated effect down the pipe a little bit because next year we will not only be missing the $60 million we are missing this year but we will be missing the inflation rate, plus the $60 million, plus the 12 per cent that $60 million would have accounted for in next year's budget. Over the four year program the total difference that $60 million will make amounts to a quarter of a billion dollars. The failure to provide these funds calls into question the whole viability of the re-equipment program.
If the capital budget does not get the funds to grow in the early years of the five year program, then there will be insufficient money to buy either the new fighters or the new ships for the navy. The minister a year ago said, when he was talking about this 12 per cent and it was in the estimates that we were discussing, that by careful housekeeping he expected he would be able to get through the year with only a 12 per cent increase. Well, he does not have 12 per cent, he only has 2.8 per cent, and obviously something is going to be cut short, particularly if we go for the more expensive airborne warning and control system and we continue to have exchange problems that eat up part of the budget. It makes the statement made by the minister about spending between $3 and $10 billion on new ships over the next 15 to 20 years appear completely ludicrous. If he cannot keep a program on course for the second year of its five year life, how can anyone be expected to take his remarks seriously for the longer term?
In closing, there are a couple of other items I feel I would be remiss if I did not mention. One is the advent of such modern weapons as the neutron bomb and the cruise missile. If the cruise missile is accepted by the various nations in the world, particularly our nation, then one has to consider a defence against the cruise missile, which the Warsaw Pact nations will have in a very short space of time. The same thing applies to the neutron bomb. However, there is no room in our acquisition plans to have a defence against the cruise missile. It might be a good reason, if the services are looking for a reason that makes more sense than the manned bomber, to have fighter aircraft that could be used against cruise missiles brought in by bombers but fired from offshore, which they are quite capable of doing. It is called stand-off firing.
The neutron bomb, which the minister likes to refer to as enhanced radiation and reduced blast, is a very, very dirty weapon. It kills people by radiation, and any advantage it might have we will lose in a couple of years. We cannot expect to stay ahead of the U.S.S.R. for very long on neutron bombs. France has claimed to have exploded one just yesterday, and someone-probably someone from the media-said that that put them ten years ahead of the Russians.
The Budget-Mr. Neil
This reminds me of the attitude just before Russia put the first Sputnik around the earth. Everybody thought that the Americans were ahead of Russia only to find that, indeed, they were a little bit behind. I would be very surprised if we were more than two years ahead of the Soviet Union in the neutron bomb area. From what I know about the neutron bomb, it is not difficult to make, and I am sure if the western allies were to accept this weapon they would not hold the advantage for very long.
I personally hope that President Carter will keep up his stand on it. His allies have told him to prepare it and build it and then give it away as a negotiating item. That may make some sense, but arming ourselves with it is not something I would like to see Canadian troops do. We have been opposed to nuclear weapon armament for quite some time now, and I do not think that the neutron bomb is worth losing our reputation over.
I would like now to say a few words about the peackeeping force which has gone to the Middle East. It was sent off by the government, and I expect it is filling a desperate need there as a communications unit. Canadians are very, very skilled in this area of providing administrative troops.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be relatively brief as I want to cover only two topics. The first is the provisions regarding family farm corporations and the second concerns registered retirement savings plans.
Under the rules that exist at the present time, there is provision for a roll-over on the death of a farmer of land to his child or children and also an inter vivos roll-over during the lifetime of the farmer provided the property was used, immediately before the transfer, by his spouse or any of his children in the business of farming.
The budget that was presented on April 10 provides for a roll-over in the case of family farm corporations. This is a welcome provision and one which members on this side of the House have sought for several years. On the prairies there are many, many family farm corporations. They take different forms and were set up for various purposes. What the budget does is provide for the transfer of shares in family farm corporations either on death or during the lifetime of the farmer to a son or daughter or, of course, any child, which includes grandchildren. This is a welcome amendment.
One thing which gives me and members of the accounting and legal professions some concern, as well as members of family farm corporations, is the uncertainty of the interpretation of this change. There is no problem where the family farm corporation owns the land, but there is a problem where the corporation, which is owned, say, by the father and one or more of his children simply rents the land from the father or a member or members of the corporation.

April 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Neil
This is a fairly common situation in corporate set-ups, particularly within the province of Saskatchewan. Because of capital gains tax and other features, in many instances it is deemed wise that the father retain ownership of the land and rent it to the corporation. Where the grey area exists is in the interpretation. What is the position if the father and his sons are members of the corporation and that corporation is farming rented land, is the property in question immediately before death or transfer being used by the farmer, his spouse or his children as a farming operation?
This situation has caused a great deal of concern since the budget was introduced. From the interpretation made by some top tax experts, I understand their feeling is that the way the budget reads and the ways and means motion reads, in instances where the land is being rented by a corporation then there can be no tax-free roll-over.
I would ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the government to give this matter careful thought with the idea of clarifying the situation. It places the farmer in a situation where, if he is renting land and wants to dispose of it, he has no alternative but to cancel the lease with the corporation. He or his child or children would then operate it for one year and at that point would effect the roll-over. It seems ridiculous to have to go that route but that is the situation. I would urge the minister to take steps to see that the matter is clarified and, if necessary, changes are made to provide that the regulations will be equitable.
I should like to say a few words now about registered retirement savings plans, Mr. Speaker. Many individuals throughout Canada who have an RRSP appreciate the changes proposed in the budget which would provide more flexibility than there has been in the past. They allow for an annuity to be purchased till age 90 rather than a life annuity to be purchased at age 71. They also provide for some flexibility with respect to the type of RRSP that an individual can have.
A number of people have expressed concern to me about being tied to this age 90 annuity or the life annuity at age 71. They say, in many instances, that they have been saving all their lives anticipating that when they retire they will be able to take a trip with some of the money they have saved. Many people do travel at age 70 to 75 when their health is still good. They want to know why it is not possible to have flexibility in the plan that would enable them, when they reach age 70, to draw larger amounts out of the plan for, say, the first three or four years in order that they could take a few trips and enjoy their retirement.
It cannot be said that the government would lose any tax as a result of a flexible program such as this. If the moneys were withdrawn from time to time they would be taxable. If the government is concerned that the individual who withdraws the money might not pay the tax or might spend the money and have none with which to pay tax, they could deduct, say, 15 per cent of the amount withdrawn in each of the years and the company could remit that amount to the tax department.

These people are concerned because in many cases they have saved all their lives in anticipation of getting some enjoyment out of their twilight years. I suggest that the Minister of Finance look carefully at the regulations to see if he can make some arrangements for greater flexibility to allow these people to determine the amount they can withdraw from the program, at least in the first three or four years after reaching age 71.

In this particular budget there are certain items of interest to people in British Columbia. I think the item most in demand is the one concerning board and lodging benefits and tax-free benefits for all employees at remote work sites. Remote work sites are sites where people cannot be expected to build or maintain a home in the ordinarily considered way. People live on these sites and as well they have homes in various parts of the country. They maintain their families and they put their children in school and then go off to the remote site. This particular provision has made it possible for employees in these remote areas to receive tax-free benefits.
Of course, there were other items in the budget to stimulate the economy and assist the recovery of this country. Because of this industrial growth will be increased. To strengthen consumer buying, to get goods moving and to create more jobs is really what everyone is seeking in a budget in an admittedly difficult time. To do this it would be advisable to cut taxes, and cutting taxes is a popular art especially just before an election. There are those who cynically believe that one would do just about anything before an election in order to have a favourable result. I think that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has put that to rest in a very outstanding way by gaining the co-operation of the provinces, even if it has been made into a somewhat politicized issue.
I feel that my colleagues and indeed many Canadians are willing to congratulate the Minister of Finance for his respon-
April 20, 1978

sibility and clear-sightedness in preparing this budget for us. I am particularly impressed as a northerner from the far west of this country that the budget did include, as I stated, a number of measures that will be of direct and immediate benefit for the kind of Canadians 1 represent.
It is from that perspective that I wish to enter this current budget debate, from the perspective of one who cares deeply about the people who live in the far reaches of Canada outside of our major cities. There are two matters that I wish to draw attention to. First, I would like to highlight what this budget, together with other economic measures taken by this government, will mean for the far west and north, areas of critical importance to Canada because of the part their vast mineral and other wealth plays in our balance of trade. Second, I want to look at economic performance in these areas during the tenure of our current Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and under the influence of comprehensive Liberal economic policies.
For the benefit of members of the opposition with short attention spans, and sometimes I am afraid minimal comprehension, let me give short answers first. On the impact of this budget, I say that its measures will mean increased activity in many sectors of the economy which are particularly important to the west and to the north. This is true for logging, farming and for exploration sectors, as it is for many others.
On recent economic performance, I can say that the west and north have seen excellent progress and performance in most sections, even in the face of global economic upset during part of the last decade. In this regard, almost every economic indicator of importance shows significant real advances. In addition, the federal government has co-operated with the provinces in undertaking projects that will build the infrastructure of this nation. The positive results are obvious for anyone who looks objectively at the figures available.
I will come back later to these points about healthy economic performance in the west and north and will fully document them for you, Mr. Speaker, and for hon. members of the House. First, I want to deal with the positive impact which many of this budget's measures, together with accompanying measures that augment the budget's effectiveness, will have on the economy of this part of Canada over the coming years.
I think it is important that we see this budget in its context of other economic initiatives taken by this particular government. A budget is an important tool of economic management. I remind hon. members, however, that it is, after all, only one tool. Its many positive programs and elements serve to support and advance a whole range of programs designed to build this country and to increase the prosperity of Canadians everywhere. The opposition makes the dishonest ploy of selectively focusing on certain elements of the budget, when it is the rest of the budget and the rest of this government's far-reaching economic programs that are really part of the whole picture. It is fashionable on the other side to make selective statements as if other things did not exist.
The Budget-Mrs. Campagnolo
