The hon. member opposite forgets that he reads almost everything he utters except his ad libs, and I wish he would stand up when he makes them.
Let me be more specific about the positive impact of measures contained in this budget and in current programs to stimulate the economy and build for the future. In remote logging and construction camps such as I mentioned earlier in my remarks before six o'clock, wage earners will receive higher after-tax income as a result of the measure to remove the value of board and lodging in relation to earnings. Not only will this put more money into the pockets of a sizeable number of men and women, people who are consumers as well as workers, but it will help employers to attract and keep those employees engaged in these projects which contribute so substantially to Canada's industrial growth.
There is also a particularly good bit of news in the budget for the many farmers who have steadfastly maintained the tradition of family farms and who have incorporated their holdings. The announcement that tax-free roll-overs will be extended to include incorporated family farms means that the tradition of family-owned and operated farms is being protected and encouraged. This provision will be very significant for the many farmers outside the large acreage farm belts of central Canada, but in my part of the country it is only the most recent of a whole range of government initiatives designed to facilitate agricultural development.
In July of last year the Prime Minister and Premier Bennett announced a joint program aimed at agricultural and rural development which will pump more than $80 million into agriculture in the province of B.C. over the next five years. It is a comprehensive program which will help small agricultural communities develop facilities for serving the farm community. It will rehabilitate extensive range lands, provide money for market and other research and fund such projects as new irrigation systems. This, together with the budget announcement, is a convincing commitment to the future of small scale agriculture in Canada as well as to large scale corporate agricultural groups.
But the commitment to agriculture in the west and north and Canada at large does not end there. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) recently announced plans to build additional grain handling facilities in Prince Rupert to take the pressure off Vancouver and to facilitate the movement of grain from northern Alberta to a northern export port. The commitment to rail upgrading, to the provision of additional rolling stock, and to aggressive overseas marketing-an effort that has consistently produced record sales-all form part of the comprehensive plan for economic development in this sector.
The current budget makes brief but telling reference to mining. I know it is popular to deride the future of mining among the doomsayers across the way. It is a sector on which much of this country's wealth is built. I believe the federal and provincial financial and resource ministers are in the process of reviewing the taxation of the mineral industry, with an eye to its continued health and importance.
This process of careful review is taking place against a background of active involvement by governments in developing the infrastructures that will make rapid mineral development possible when world markets inevitably draw on Canada's huge potentials in this area. Two examples of this approach can be found in the joint agreements between the federal government and the government of B.C. in developing coal and uranium resources in the province. In January, 1977, we signed an agreement that put $3 million into transportation, manpower, community resources, and environmental studies. It was followed in May, 1977, by a second agreement that will make available $10 million for the same purpose over the next three years. These agreements are in addition, Mr. Speaker, to projects such as Roberts Bank-in which I know the hon. member in the back row opposite is interested-which has already made a huge contribution to the B.C. economy.
In April, 1976, we joined with the province in funding regional geochemical exploration in B.C.-specifically aimed at identifying and developing uranium resources.

My colleagues have gone into some detail in explaining the positive impact that can be expected subsequent to a cut in sales tax. In British Columbia the federal government will fund a 2 per cent cut in the cost of consumer items. That, I believe, will be a signal to consumers to buy, with a range of spin-off benefits for retail merchants, wholesalers and manufacturers.
But again, if one were just to look at this element of government economic measures, one would not see their comprehensive and integrated nature. To use the example again of the more remote parts of B.C., the federal government is co-operating with the province in funding an ambitious five year industrial development program that will pump up to $110 million into its economy. The money is available to help fund the construction of such things as industrial parks to assist municipalities in attracting businesses. Other money is directly available to manufacturing, service and small business ventures and other similar industries. The money will fund industrial commissions, which in turn are eligible for money for market research, research that will help to establish the potential of these remote areas in British Columbia.
To aid the fishing industry on the west coast, there has been a considerable amount of funding, research and a great deal of work undertaken. My colleague the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) has undertaken an ambitious

The $100 million plus salmonoid enhancement scheme has already yielded results in the form of above average catches on the Nass and Skeena rivers in the past year. This is a fact that augurs well for the future of this most important industry, an industry that is currently valued at more than $300 million at the wholesale level.
The introduction of the 200-mile fisheries protection limit, together with the reduction of the number of foreign vessels in our waters, promises to increase the volume of the catch for Canadians, the numbers of jobs for Canadians, and the strength of the Canadian economy as a result of the increasingly significant contribution this industry will make to our balance of trade.
These elements of the budget and related economic measures, as I said at the outset, will mean increased activity in all of the sectors I have mentioned, certainly in the short run but, more important, over the long run. These are measures that build for the future-and that is what good government rather than opportunistic government is all about.
I also promised in my introductory remarks to look at the economic record of B.C. over the sweep of the last ten eventful years. I am pleased to be able to say that according to most indices, the economy in that part of Canada has paralleled the growth of the economy in all of Canada-it has steadily advanced. In the last couple of years, B.C.'s economy has actually outpaced that in the rest of Canada because it has been the direct beneficiary of a number of federal government programs I have already touched on, and because certain B.C. industries have benefitted from the very phenomenon the Conservatives are so strongly denouncing-the devaluation of the dollar.
I will speak more about our current economic status and about our immediate prospects in a few moments, but first let me dig into the past. The Conservatives would have Canadians believe that we are all a lot worse off than we were when the Prime Minister came to office ten years ago. If one were to believe those prophets of despair, Canadians are less productive, less well fed and less prosperous than before. One would expect less investment, lower production volumes and a lower standard of living. But that is not the case, and I will present a few figures to make my point.
First, let me indicate some sweeping indicators as guides to our economic progress: gross provincial product, new capital investment and the value of exports. In 1967 British

New capital investment in 1967 was about $2.6 billion in British Columbia. Last year it was $7.2 billion, which is roughly a 250 per cent increase. With the exception of 1968, real investment figures have increased every year, jumping by close to a billion dollars a year over the last two years, each year. It is jumping by close to a billion dollars each year.
The value of exports leaving British Columbia was about $2 billion in 1967. Last year it was $8.4 billion, which is a 430 per cent increase. Also this figure has taken enormous strides during the last couple of years.
The record in these three critical areas puts the lie to Conservative babblings about hard times. Of course we have problems, all nations have problems, but what are we doing? We are doing a lot more than just coping. We are advancing at a rate that most other countries would like dearly to emulate.
If hon. members think I have deliberately stacked the deck by choosing just a few especially good figures tonight, while more gloomy ones go unmentioned, let me point out significant advances on other scales as well. Retail sales advanced from $2.6 billion in 1967 to $3.3 billion in 1970; to $4.6 billion in 1973; to more than $7 billion in 1977. This is more than a 200 per cent increase in ten years. Mineral production values jumped from $380 million in 1967 to $530 million in 1971; to $1.3 billion in 1974; to $1.8 billion in 1977. This is another 400 per cent increase. The landed value of British Columbia fish catches has recorded a 300 per cent increase in the decade. It advanced from $50 million in 1967 to $150 million last year. Remember this is the landed value of the catch. At the wholesale level the value of the catch passed the $300 million mark last year.
The lumber industry has been more variable over the decade, because it is more subject to market conditions in other countries than most. When building starts are down in the United States, the Canadian lumber industry suffers as a result. But in that decade the number of board feet of production advanced from about 7.1 billion board feet to roughly 12 billion. The industry has more than recovered from the bad years of 1974 and 1975 and is looking forward to an excellent year in 1978.

I can see some hon. members opposite starting to wince, as they do when they hear some true figures for a change, so let me conclude my numbers by pointing to progress in British Columbia in a field the opposition has chosen as its very own-employment. If we were to believe the Conservatives and members of the New Democratic Party, no progress should have been made in securing livelihoods for British Columbia residents or, in fact, from listening to them during question period, for any Canadians whatsoever.
The figures indicate the following: between 1967 and 1977 more than 354,000 jobs were created in the province of British Columbia. Employment is currently at an all time high, with 1,065,000 men and women gainfully employed in that province. The rate of job creation shows every sign of soon outstripping the truly phenomenal rate of increase in participation in the work force. When that takes place, as it will because of the promising national and world economic picture a few months and years down the road, then the economic stimuli wisely implemented by this government will ensure that unemployment rates return to the very low levels all Canadians have a right to expect.
If hon. members still think I am overly optimistic or perhaps a little selective, let me conclude by pointing to the economic prospectus for British Columbia which was prepared by the Employers Council of British Columbia. This was prepared for the coming year. That council is predicting a real growth rate of 5 per cent for 1978. It foresees strong markets for our products in all nations, but most importantly, those nations which are on our specific list, such as Japan. There are other nations which are of interest to our western economy, such as the countries of the European Economic Community and the United States. The council predicts strong years for the fishing industry, the tourist industry, the oil and gas industry and for a number of key mineral industries. The legacy of the controls program is part of the significantly improved labour scene, and it will make the predictions possible. The Employers Council thinks this will continue for another year, and we will see

vastly fewer days lost to strikes and lockouts, as we have experienced since the program of anti-inflation began.
I am proud of the record of this government. As I have said and supported, I have particular cause for satisfaction as a resident of northwestern Canada. I ask Canadians to look at what the record really contains, and to give the doom and gloom portraits of the oppositions the scorn they deserve. Once again, I make mention of the hon. Minister of Finance. As I said a few moments ago, good government rather than opportunistic government is something special. Good government is what we have. It has done and will do more for the average Canadian than the nay-saying, crepe hanging of hon. members opposite. This government is led truly and surely by a rational, logical, intelligent leader; not someone who has to bear the indignity of a teeny, tiny perfect threat to his opposition leadership.
We are a team on this side of the House. We have a leader of whom we are very proud and one whom the world respects. Respect is what I am talking about tonight. I am not only speaking of leadership, I am also speaking of the solid, year-in, year-out service to human beings that members of the government spend their time on. Hon. members on this side of the House stand for service to the people of this nation, whether an individual in Canada, a group with special interests, be they large or small, or a lot of Canadians seeking changes to adapt to a new and sometimes very frightening future. This is a government of service, as well as a government of leadership.
This was a budget of service, and the budget debate on this side of the House has shown what kinds of services are offered to hundreds of thousands of Canadians.

We have been listening to various government members during this budget debate, and one might think one was not living in the reality that is known as Canada today. For example, it has been mentioned time after time that investment in this country is not being made in order to create the number of jobs that we need, first of all simply to maintain the present unemployment rate, to say nothing of reducing it.
The hon. minister spoke for half an hour and at no time did she ever refer to the crisis that is now facing us in Canada as a result of the one million unemployed. She acted as if the situation did not exist, and as though there were not one million unemployed. She never mentioned that. Nor did she mention that there are young Canadians under the age of 25 today who, upon entering the labour force, have doubled the national unemployment average. Never did she mention that there were students coming into the labour market at the end

Let us look at the facts as presented by impartial observers-for example, the Conference Board of Canada. Its report today stated that barely three months ago, in January, Canada's real growth after inflation was estimated at 4.7 per cent.
It is generally regarded that we need 5 per cent real growth just to maintain present growth, and with that we will not even have started to reduce the unemployment rate. Three months after making that projection the Conference Board today lowered that projection to 3.9 per cent. The fact of the matter is that we do not have enough growth in this country at this point in time to give to our young people and our unemployed the opportunities they deserve.
We could look at the loss of investment capital in Canada. At no time did a member of the cabinet get up and say what the government was going to do simply to reduce the exodus of investment capital from this country. Every time investments of this kind are made outside the country two things are obvious: the first is that many Canadians do not have confidence in this government and are, therefore, investing outside Canada; they do not have confidence in the economic leadership of this country. That is simple.
Even more important-and this is a long term effect-is the fact that as we invest outside Canada we do not invest to create the jobs we need now. Right now we are exporting jobs. As western Canadians we have chafed for a long time over this situation. We have said that in our view we have not realized our economic potential because of exporting raw materials without enough processing at home. Members from western Canada regardless of their political persuasion have put this argument forward. The situation has gone even further in that we have now reached the point where we are exporting jobs not just out of western Canada but simply out of Canada. That is a very tragic situation.
What I want to do today is bring to the attention of the House some of the realities of Canada and some of the opportunities that I believe exist. Earlier the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) quoted from a statement by the Prime Minister of England, Mr. Callaghan, in which he stated that one cannot create prosperity by government spending, and one cannot create prosperity by spending oneself out of trouble. I agree with that statement. You cannot spend more than you produce for a long period of time without reaping the negative effects of that economic approach.
This is the situation we are facing in Canada today. The huge deficits being rolled up by this government will not be paid by any member of this House. They will be paid through lost jobs lost opportunities and high taxes on our children and their children. The legacy of spending by this government is now becoming a legacy of debt for future generations. The future generations will be saddled with this debt. There is no point in minimizing that fact. It is simply a fact that exists.
We have seen from the British Columbia and Manitoba experiences that it is very difficult for a provincial or a federal government to cut back. I am not suggesting for a minute this is easy or that it is a panacea. However, it does take leadership, and this government has not shown leadership in putting in place those programs needed to create expansion. It has in fact continued a process that has cost great amounts of money, but from which we have received very little in long term economic benefits.
The government has not emphasized the spending of public funds on job creation on a long term basis within the private sector. Every government that is now faced with deadlock- whether a federal, provincial or municipal government-is faced with the startling reality that they cannot continue spending the amounts of money that they have been spending in the past. What the government intends to do, according to the budget statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is spend $1 billion a month more than it takes in in any given month over the next year. The government expects to have a deficit of SI 1.5 billion, roughly a $1 billion shortfall a month. They intend to over-spend this year more than the total budget for the first year of the government of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when it stood at $9.9 billion. Today the over-spending exceeds that by one and a half million dollars.
I ask the members of this House, is that economic leadership? Is that courage? Is that an economic statement that is worthy of praise, or economic leadership that one can go to the Canadian people with and say "Look how well we have led"? The point that I am making is that it will be difficult for any government to cut back. Why is it difficult? The minute a program is established it creates within itself a dependency factor which benefits certain areas but does not necessarily benefit the total economy or all of the Canadian people. I challenge every government in Canada today to get their economic house in order. It is going to mean difficult decisions. There are going to be negative reactions from many people who feel that they are being done in by that kind of program; but it is a program that is extremely necessary if we are to give to our children and grandchildren a heritage that will allow them to develop the potential that I believe is Canada.
I would like to spend some time on the matter of farm income. One of the most incredible statements that I have heard in this House was made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) the other day. I quote him from Hansard at page 4641, April 18, 1978:
I am so tired of hearing talk about farmers who have lost their net income. I wonder how many are honest enough to admit why farm land is higher in value in Canada than it is in the United States. The answer should be plain and simple to them. It is because farm income is generally better in Canada and because farmers, if they are efficient producers, are provided more security in this country that they are in any other nation of the world. None of our programs provide any kind of income for an inefficient producer who is lazy and does not want to work. He or she must work or they will not get that kind of living or that kind of net income I have just talked about.

April 20, 1978

He further said:
I am so tired of listening to politicians and even some farm leaders who talk about farm income going down. I received a letter from a so-called farm leader from British Columbia pointing out that the farmers' incomes had dropped 9 per cent. Mr. Speaker, do you know how much farm income went up in 1975? At that time it had an increase of 187 per cent.
That is what is recorded in Hansard, but what are the facts. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture in its statement to members of parliament dated April, 1978 said:
If the 1978 figure is reduced 19 per cent to 1975 dollars, it becomes $1,562 billion, a drop from 1975 of an horrendous 54 per cent.
How can the Minister of Agriculture say there is an increase of 187 per cent when the Canadian Federation of Agriculture-and I would think that those members who have a rural riding know that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is a very credible organization-comes out with this report?
I went a little further, Mr. Speaker, because I wanted to find out what was happening in Manitoba. Here are the figures, taken from Statistics Canada data as compiled by the Manitoba Credit Union Federation. They are not my compilation, so it cannot be argued I used wrong addition or sleight-of-hand. In 1976 the gross income of Canadian farmers was $9,975 million. The expenditures of farmers in 1976 in Canada gave them a net income of $3,706 million. In 1977 that net income was reduced to $3,372 million, and in 1978 it is estimated that there will be a further drop to $3,082 million. Even a zero growth I would understand, but not 187 per cent.
Let me now go to Manitoba, because that is the province I was most interested in. In 1976 Manitoba farmers had a gross income of $897 million and costs of $570 million, for a net income of $327 million. In 1977 their income was $892 million, and costs of $611 million gave them a net income of $281 million, a drop from 1976. The estimate for this year from the same statistics is that income will escalate to $904 million with a comparative cost increase of $656 million. It is estimated, Mr. Speaker, that their income will drop even further to between $248 and $260 million. How can the Minister of Agriculture say that there has been an increase? He cannot use the figures of gross income without looking at input costs, because surely, every person in this House and every farmer in this country must look at income as income after expenses. Surely no other figure is valid. I say to the Minister of Agriculture, almost in disillusion rather than anger, that Canadian farmers are in desperate straits because of the cost-price squeeze they are in.
Let us look at some of the solutions. In Manitoba we have a program in the Interlake region known as the ARDA program. The ARDA program, and I say this quite openly, I believe had beneficial effects in the Interlake. The program in the Interlake was used for drainage and land clearance, with a general approach to expanding the agricultural base. At that time we in southeastern Manitoba were hoping that our area would also be included in the special ARDA region. Conditions were similar. Unfortunately, this was not to take place.
The Budget-Mr. Epp
What has happened, not through my leadership but through that of farmers and local municipal officials in the far southeastern corner of Manitoba, is that they have created a development corporation known as the Stuartburn-Piney Agriculture Development Association. A large portion of the land mass of this area is Crown land, and primarily provincial Crown land. The province is working on a plan in conjunction with the farmers so that they can sell some of this bona fide Crown land to farmers in order to expand the agricultural base. I hope that plan will be put into effect shortly.
A survey was done in that area by these constituents and it showed some very interesting facts. It showed that there was not enough developed land for an agricultural base that would have economic viability. It showed that people in the area were interested in land development and in making the investment, and that what they needed was an incentive program. Three-quarters of the respondents to the survey indicated that drainage and water control was a problem. The underlying argument, however, was that they needed to expand the tax base and create an infrastructure.
I think a few facts should be put on record about the findings of this committee, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to quote from the study as follows:
The farmers of the L.G.D. of Stuartburn and Piney suffer from the lowest farm incomes and poor agricultural services in the province of Manitoba ...
65 per cent earn $1200 to $5000 gross. There are several reasons for this:
(1) Very small percentage of total land, only 4 per cent and 7 per cent respectively in Piney and Stuartburn is developed crop land. In most cases, a lot more land can be developed and put into agricultural production ...
What they propose-and I want to present this to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) and the Minister of Agriculture-is the following. I believe the first recommendation is the critical one. It reads as follows:
First we propose that this area be designated for assistance under a long term federal-provincial ARDA-type program bearing some of the following points in mind:
Then they clearly spell out the various advantages that program would have and the areas of development they would like to see take place.
I listened to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion state today that he would be signing an agreement with the government of the province of Manitoba tomorrow. I urge and recommend to him that first of all we need a general development agreement for the southeastern part of Manitoba. That agreement should not only include tourism, which is an attractive option for that area, but should definitely include a program similar to the special ARDA area that was used in the Interlake. At the present time the minister of agriculture for the province of Manitoba has associated himself with this report. He wants to move ahead and we look forward to the co-operation of the federal minister in this program. I ask the minister not to worry about press releases and announcements that an agreement will be signed tomorrow, but to put into that agreement terms which will allow for the development of this area and the growth that these people deserve.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) that she was better in her former portfolio than the present one. I also say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that if she is still interested in the problem, highway 59 should be open for a longer period of time as a port of entry. This is important. Communities along that highway have asked for it. Chambers of commerce such as St. Pierre have asked for it, but there has been no positive response from the federal government.
There are other areas of eastern Manitoba where I believe potential exists and can be developed. There is the old question of the northlands agreement. That was signed and was to be a general development agreement to expand economic activity in the north. We have seen very little positive effect from it. I say to the government and to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion that a development program is needed throughout eastern Manitoba. We must get a program that does not just spend money on research and more studies. We have been literally studied to death. I say, use some of the money for development.
Let me give an example of what I mean, Mr. Speaker. I mentioned to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) that research and development should be expanded, for instance, into tantalum mining in eastern Manitoba. We have at least 66 per cent of the world's reserves of cesium tantalum. We were exporting some to the U.S.S.R. so we placed it on the export control list. I am not arguing the point that it should be placed on the export control list. We have a potential there. But instead of expanding research and development, instead of expanding opportunities for ancillary manufacturing that could come from that mining, we literally closed the place down and said that if we cannot export it to our traditional markets, nothing will happen.
I should like now to speak of small business, and this takes me to the matter of taxation. A great deal was said in the budget about the reduction of sales tax by the federal government. I say quite openly that it is hoped the reduction of sales tax will have a beneficial effect on retail sales in Canada, at least for the next six months. What will happen when we go into the winter period and the tax comes back is another question.
I want to point out what happens between the time something is presented to us in the House and the person back home is faced with the regulations which flow from decisions made here. In the March 31, 1977, budget there was a provision for a roll-over if a person sold his farm or small business and used the full amount of money to buy another farm. In that case there was to be a deferment of capital gains

tax. That was really the essence of the program. I announced it in my riding and in the budget debate I supported the provision. Indeed, most hon. members commended the government for that action.
I find things a little strange now, however. First the government puts on a capital gains tax and then removes it in certain instances in two subsequent budgets. A case was brought to my attention of a farmer who had land and a poultry operation. He decided to sell the poultry operation and rolled the total proceeds over to purchase more land to expand his grain operation. Revenue Canada taxed him. It was never mentioned in this House that if a farmer-let us say a hog producer- should sell his hog operation and buy a larger operation that was not a hog operation, he would be taxed. That is trickery. That is what creates the cynicism that we find about government throughout Canada.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lumley) is here this evening. I have mentioned this situation to his minister and to the Minister of Agriculture. I thought last week that we were making some progress and that that regulation, which I found out in fact does exist, would be modified. I had high hopes that common sense would prevail. But what do I find out this week? I found out that a farmer can sell a farm, say a dairy farm, and use that money for a rollover only if he buys a larger dairy farm. If he buys a grain farm, he will be taxed.
Was that the way it was presented to the people of Canada on March 31, 1977? No way. I say to them, Mr. Speaker, that is the ignominy that this government will have to face with the farmers and the small businessmen of Canada. No matter how you cut it, it was not presented to them in that way. I say to the farmers and the small businessmen of this country that if that regulation is not removed with the provisions that were in the March 31, 1977 budget and this recent budget, then they had better be careful before they make any move whatsoever.
I notice that the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) is in the House tonight. He has made a few pronouncements that small business is going to get the government off its back; less red tape, less bureaucracy, more return. I say to the minister that I hope he is right. I hope that what he has said will in fact take place and that I will not have to come back to him a few months later-

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) closed his remarks by touching on a particular interpretation of a regulation and its enforcement. He then immediately drew from that example a conclusion, the wrong one. But instead of waiting and pursuing the interpretation, pursuing it not only through gov-
April 20, 1978

ernment but also through the various processes which are available, he drew an interpretation of skepticism and cynicism which is so common in those who constantly oppose.
The record of this government is clear as being sympathetic to the various needs and situations in which our Canadian farmers find themselves in regard to their taxes. This budget included a new move in relation to the extension of the rollover of the capital gains tax to the corporate farm structure. Those of us on this side of the House who saw the need for the rollover for farmers in the first place thought that it would apply fairly broadly. We found as a matter of interpretation that the way the law was written it did not apply to corporations. We were first told there might be some difficulties in applying it in that regard. We persisted and we saw that the change was in fact extended.
That is not the first example by any means of the extension of tax advantages to farmers. I would remind the hon. member for Provencher that when it came to the question of delivery of grain and how that grain would be delivered, it was this government which quickly responded to a need on the prairies, where the quota system exists and where farmers were in the position of not necessarily being able to control deliveries, for a new device-the idea of preferred tax credit where they could deliver their grain and have the grain counted in the following year for tax purposes, if that is what they chose.
Those are just small examples, but important ones, of the way this government has been responsive to the needs of that sector of agriculture to which the hon. member for Provencher most recently referred.
It is extraordinary that the hon. member today would talk about agriculture and its needs when the record of the Conservative party, even when it was represented by large numbers of members from the west, was such a sorry story in the area of agriculture. It is most extraordinary indeed.
Hon. members opposite, including several from Saskatchewan and other prairie provinces, were critical when an analysis of all the developments which have taken place in agriculture in the last eight or nine years went out not long ago from this government. It was a long document with many items in it of tremendous importance to farmers, and particularly to grain farmers to whom it was addressed. It included such things as hopper cars, with an expenditure of $250 million for that item. It included the introduction of two-price wheat. It included grain stabilization which the Tories have so long fought to stop from coming into existence, not because in their hearts they thought it was unwise, but because they did not want to see a program of that quality put in place by a Liberal government with the Liberals taking credit for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

speechtext:
The budget of the Minister of Finance was a courageous budget, one which was welcomed by economic experts across this country as being the right thing for today,
The extraordinary testimony about the quality of the budget of the Minister of Finance is the fact that some members suspect, probably with some correctness, that we are fairly close to election time. It could have been very tempting for the Minister of Finance to accept a suggestion that more be done in the way of tax cuts, that he not restrain himself to the $1.2 billion in total tax cuts being accomplished in these next six months by his reduction in sales tax, whereby he helps the provinces to create those reductions. He could have done more about that if he had not been careful about the advice of his best advisers or not cared about the comment and advice of reasonable experts everywhere.
What in the face of that budget do the opposition parties come up with at a time when there are challenges and you might think they would be dreaming solutions of their own? The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) comes in with a motion that suggests there be a tax cut of $2 billion on the income tax side. Essentially the New Democratic Party through the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Salts-man) said that a sales tax cut is the right cut. In neither party were there imaginative ideas about what the government should do in the way of further job creation. There was no criticism, particularly of our Canada Works programs, our other major ventures and all the rest.
There were a few comments by the opposition about matters chosen from the first ministers' conference and the background papers, such as the economic development which we see ahead and where 11 first ministers agreed that the course the government was on was right. Hon. members opposite then say there should be a tax cut of $2 billion a year. What the Minister of Finance came up with was a tax cut of $1.2 billion in six to nine months, which is a greater tax cut than they with their best imagination are able to come up with as economic advice today.
The evidence was clear that this was the right thing to do. Economic advice clearly indicated that was the best course available to this government. The banks, the senior civil service and all outside advice agreed as well, so much so that the opposition did not dare to suggest, even in their own position of opposition, that much more should have been done in that regard.
One might well ask where the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) gets his economic advice. The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) is now moving out of that scene, probably because he sees that not very much in the way of economic quality and advice is required or wanted by the Leader of the Opposition.

some years ago who, looking across at one particular member of the opposition, referred to him as a yahoo. That word created some parliamentary difficulty in those days. Things are different now. Look at what he thinks of advice inside the government. Whereas the Minister of Finance was accepting the best that was available, the Leader of the Opposition was sneering at it, just as he sneered at the RCMP and police of this country a few months ago when his party, instead of calling them in or having the key sleuth in his party call them in, fearing their offices were being bugged, did not trust the police. In all their attacks on the police, they could not get away from the fact that they have not trusted the best possible advice available in that circumstance, just as they do not here in economic circumstances.

They called in a group from outside, a group the quality of which is now a matter of public record. I remember one great day in Saskatoon. The morning edition of the Star Phoenix had a picture of the Leader of the Opposition peering at his telephone. There were some words to the effect that "Clark finds some listening device there". It turned out to be a top head diode, a regular part of the equipment. The afternoon edition of the Star Phoenix had much the same picture, much the same front page. It changed the headline. It read "Clark device normal". That was very reassuring to many of us. Those who believe in a healthy opposition were certainly delighted to see that bit of evidence.
The sales tax was the right tax. One of the delightful things in the Minister of Finance's introduction of this particular sales tax is that once again he was able to demonstrate the way this government seeks the support of all the country in taking what is indeed a differential approach in the way a tax is handled.
The Atlantic provinces have less financial capability than many others. In complete keeping with the spirit of this government's putting very high priority on the development of the Atlantic area and promoting causes there, the minister said there would be a 3 per cent sales tax reduction without any cost to them, fully reimbursed by the treasury. In this Liberal party, members from the west, central Canada and the Atlantic area support that kind of program, in that regard and in every regard, showing that we believe in the development of this country.
I look at the programs of this government from one part of the country to the other, programs which are designed to spur development by taking action when it is required to allow the free enterprise side of the economy to operate, which is what hon. members opposite ask.
I look at the west coast and I see our development in the ports. I see the Vanterm terminal, Lynterm, the Fairview terminal in Prince Rupert coming to a conclusion, the investment we propose to make in Ridley Island, our willingness to

co-operate through DREE in the northeast coal development. You see there, step by step, the laying of the groundwork for investment by Canadians which will mean many jobs in the future right across the country.

In the prairie provinces, I mentioned our developments in assuring grain transportation in the sense of $255 million worth of hopper cars. There are members opposite who go into other regions of the country and use that as a negative example against this government. Of course, they very much hide that from people in the prairies whom they want to support them. That is the kind of division they go through. One of their members says "Everything is done for the prairies and nothing is done for us here". They are always dividing the country instead of trying to see the positive side of good action in every region.
The stabilization program was an example of recognition by this government on the tariff structure in this country, which we are trying to improve by lowering the burden it traditionally imposed upon our prairie farmers. There was built into our structure such things as the Crowsnest rate on grain, built in and maintained because of the problems the grain farmer faces in this tariff world. We carried through on that, instead of doing nothing, as the Tories had done in their years of power, with, I say again in astonishment, a prairie prime minister and a House full of prairie Conservatives. They did nothing of note for that particular farmer.
It is a monument of credit to this country and to real democrats within it, like my Liberal colleagues from central Canada and the Altantic provinces, that when we come forward with one, two, three or four voices alone from the prairies, they do not ask whether, in providing hopper cars and $60 million a year for grain stabilization, and now $75 million a year for rail rehabilitation, there would be political consequences in our favour. They only asked whether it was right for the regions, and they were then willing to do it.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
The railway rehabilitation program is a positive example of our moving forward in an optimistic way in the prairie region in terms of the grain handling program. This program means that, with the Hall commission report and the Snavely commission report and the action now being taken,
The Budget-Mr. Lang
we shall in the course of seven or eight years have transferred to the basic rail network the bulk of the prairie grain lines and rehabilitated every one of those miles of lines with ties where required, stones to lay the ties upon which will last for half a century, and with rail which will carry those fully loaded hopper cars. That is the kind of action which is forthcoming from this government in the prairie region.
This budget also recognized the need for further railway investment. This is important in many parts of the country but particularly in the west where so much freight traffic will increasingly move. The last budget made provision for easier investment by the railways. There were cash flow advantages to the railway companies through increased depreciation allowances. One further step in that regard was taken by the Minister of Finance in this budget.

We paid that part of it which could assure railway rehabilitation in getting a contract agreement with the railways and assure that every penny was spent on equipment for those rail lines. Though not being able to go the whole distance as the commission recommended, we did put the railways in a better position be giving them depreciation advantages, and this, too, will be reflected in terms of rail development by improving the cash position of the railways.

I meant perhaps I should quit speaking. At any rate, prior to the days of the second world war, Canada was faced with a situation similar to that of today. There was a lot of unemployment in this country. People were told that money could not be found to put them back to work, to build schools, hospitals, roads and other necessary things. The government of the day indicated that it could not find a money tree. Suddenly a war broke out, and within a few short weeks, the government found money. They took men off the rails and took men out of the unemployment lines. They bought them uniforms, shined their shoes, filled their teeth and put them to work fighting a war, working in munitions factories or various factories across the country that were building tanks, boats and things for Canada's war effort. If that can be done during the time of war, surely it can be done during peacetime. We could declare war on the unemployment situation and the inequality which is present in Canada.
Many people ask what unemployment really means. It is said that it only affects a few of us, but that is not true. In the last year, unemployment has cost Canada approximately $8.5 billion. Approximately $4 billion of lost productivity, $3 billion in welfare and unemployment insurance payments and $1.5 billion in lost taxes make up that total. Instead of that money being spent on welfare and lost productivity, perhaps that amount and more should be spent on putting people to work. That would create a much better and wealthier nation for each and every one of us in the long run.
The Budget-Mr. Nystrom
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) referred to the question of rail line abandonment, which is something important to the people of the prairies. The Hall commission determined that approximately 2,000 miles of rail lines in the prairies should come under the prairie rail authority. That was suggested because a decision could not be reached as to whether or not the 2,000 miles of rail should be preserved in the basic network or abandoned. The Hall commission thought the matter required further study, and that the PRA be established for that purpose between now and 1990.
Instead of establishing a prairie rail authority, the Minister of Transport established a small advisory body composed of his friends. It is known as the Prairie Rail Action Committee. Apparently it does not have a mandate to go into various communities and hold hearings. I am referring to the communities which the Hall commission could not make a decision on. A number of those communities happen to be situated in my riding on two rail lines, namely, the rail line which runs from Preeceville to Kelvington, and the other one which runs from Canora to MacNutt. The people in those communities have set up Save Our Rail Lines committees. They want the prairie rail authority, the CTC or someone who is able, to make a decision. They want those authorities to come out to their communities to see the reason why those rail lines must be preserved. They have strong, solid arguments, and they want to present their cases to the government. The least the government can do is to instruct the Prairie Rail Action Committee, if the prairie rail authority is not going to be established, to go to those communities and hold hearings in order to provide those people with a chance to fight.
If they were provided with a chance to fight their cases in front of federal officials, I am sure they would save those rail lines. The rail lines which are placed inthe category recommended by the Hall commission deserve to be transferred to the basic rail network. I am sure the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) could point out other cases.
Before I give the hon. member for Frontenac-Lennox and Addington a chance to participate in this debate, I should like to refer to the question of farm incomes. The other day the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) indicated that Canadian farmers are enjoying quite a bit of affluence. When he quoted his figures, he forgot to mention that he was referring to farm income jumps between 1971 and 1974. He picked 1971, which was one of the worst years Canada has ever had in relation to farm incomes, and 1974, which was one of the better years.
If one refers to those two years, of course there will be a substantial increase in farm incomes. But in the last three years, farm incomes have dropped drastically. From 1975 to 1977, in fact farm incomes went down by 73 per cent in Canada. I am referring to the net farm income which goes into the pockets of farmers. At the same time farm costs have risen by 18 per cent. Farm incomes have dropped by 23 per cent at the same time as farm costs have risen by 18 per cent. Canadian farmers deserve better, but they have not received such from the hon. minister. When one looks at other statistics

During that same period of time, the cost of operating prairie farms has risen by some 23 per cent. How can a farmer be expected to pay his bills, if the costs are rising by 23 per cent and his income is dropping by 55 per cent?

It is regrettable, sir, that the policy makers of that party did not find themselves able to look beyond the next election. Sir, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in marking the end of his decade in power, having been first elected to the high office in 1968, marks the end of this decade at this time.
In 1968 when the first Trudeau government came to power, the Prime Minister campaigned under the slogan "The Just Society". If the just society meant anything in 1968, it was a clear mandate to Trudeau and the Liberals to attack regional disparities across our country, to work to alleviate poverty in our society and to improve employment conditions and fight unemployment in our society.
The slogan "The Just Society" would imply a fair system of taxation. In order for the just society to prosper, inflation should have been controlled. Again, a just society would expect the wise spending and administration of tax moneys levied from that society by this government, in whom that so called
[Mr. Nystrom.l
just society had pinned its hopes. Our society of 1968 expected continuation of healthy trade relationships with other countries and the usual measure of necessary tariff protection for Canadian industry that would be vulnerable to unfair competition from countries employing cheap labour.
That once strong society of 1968 expected that our government would be a good neighbour among the comity of nations, helping those less fortunate than ourselves as long as it was not at the expense and dire hardship of unemployment of our citizens. That just society expected a reasonably strong economy that would sustain itself if it were left alone and was not over taxed or dictated to by a federal government.
That 1968 just society I mentioned implied good co-operation and good relationships between the so-called two founding races of our country; the French and, for want of a better description, the English. We expected bilingualism would be encouraged only wherever needed in our public service, and wherever numbers warranted this and it was expected.
We anticipated that all these principles and ideas, if put into effect, would maintain the unity we had always enjoyed before this country ever heard of Prime Ministers by the names of Pearson or Trudeau. But, alas, none of those great expectations ever materialized. We are now all asking the question here this evening, even some of those on the government side, as a result of a surfeit of so-called Liberalism and ten years of Trudeau: Where is that just society? It is a myth; it simply does not exist.
Both national unity and justice have been withering and dying over the past decade. The so-called charisma that the Prime Minister was supposed to have possessed is also a myth. The Liberal administration has been a total failure and all that remains at the present time is the Prime Minister's obsession with power and the exercise of power.
To go back over the list of implications I have just mentioned in the meaning of a just society, we see that Liberalism under the Prime Minister has totally failed in this country, and we see where that failure has led us.
Sir, I must now dispense with further remarks I had ready regarding this budget and say to you and to the House that my final remarks during this budget debate tonight pertain to myself, my family and, one might say, "my budget".
As most hon. members know, after 16 years in this House as representative of the former federal riding of Prince Edward Lennox and the still existing riding of Frontenac-Lennox and Addington-that is, it still exists until an election writ is issued-I am voluntarily retiring from federal politics.
I was first elected on June 18, 1962 and I am the last remaining Progressive Conservative member of what we call the "class of '62", although there are several other members remaining in this House from other parties of that class of '62.
My working career began here in Ottawa in 1931 when I was employed by the government of that day, the Bennett government, as a clerk, grade 2, in the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. I was employed on the agricultural census for two years, and the offices of the bureau were on Green Island,
April 20, 1978

down on Sussex Avenue, directly opposite the present City Hall.
My working career as far as this House is concerned also ends here in Ottawa, in this House of Commons, where I was a frequent gallery visitor as a boy in 1931 and 1932, never thinking I would occupy a seat here for sixteen years.

speechtext: My friends, I have seen quite a bit of the Canadian Kaleidoscope pass in review in this chamber. Although I have sat on the opposition side for the past 15 years, with the goodwill and help of colleagues from both sides of this House I have been able to accomplish many things in the service of my constituents, and I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and other Speakers under whom I have served, as well as members on both side of the House.

I want to thank all hon. members of this present House and that vast throng of other members and colleagues of the past who are no longer here, many of whom have gone to their just reward. My appreciation and commendation also go out to all those who work on Parliament Hill, which of course includes the security staff, the secretaries and
The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack
the executive assistants, all of whom I remember and recognize with magnanimity and gratitude. My deep appreciation also goes to the public service and all the various departments of government that throughout the years have assisted me in representing my constituents.
I deem it time to return to Napanee, my home in Lennox and Addington county. I invite all my colleagues in any of their journeys throughout our area, or near it, to visit me in Napanee. I can assure them that they will certainly be welcome.
